title: Good, Evil & Reasons for Crime
content_html:
Good and Evil Intentions and Actions

Every action has an intention behind it. Religious believers distinguish between good intentions (those that aim to help others and follow God’s will) and evil intentions (those that aim to harm others or defy what is morally right). A key question in ethics is whether a good intention can justify an action that causes suffering.

Christians believe that God gave humans free will — the ability to choose between good and evil. This means humans are morally responsible for their actions. The Bible teaches: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31), suggesting that the world was created good but that humans can choose to act in evil ways.

In Islam, humans are also believed to have free will. Allah created humans as his khalifah (stewards) on earth, responsible for making moral choices. The Qur’an teaches that those who do good will be rewarded on the Day of Judgement, while those who do evil will be held accountable: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it” (Qur’an 99:7–8).

Key Fact

Can it ever be good to cause suffering? Some argue that causing suffering can be justified if it leads to a greater good — for example, a doctor performing painful surgery to save a life, or a parent disciplining a child to teach right from wrong. Others argue that deliberately causing suffering is always wrong because it violates the sanctity of life and human dignity. Christianity teaches “do to others what you would have them do to you” (Matthew 7:12); Islam teaches that Allah is merciful and expects humans to show mercy too.

Reasons for Crime

People commit crimes for many different reasons. Understanding why crime occurs helps society respond appropriately and helps religious believers consider how to balance justice with compassion. the specification identifies four main categories of reasons for crime.

Poverty and upbringing: People living in poverty may steal to feed their families or survive. Those raised in environments where crime is normalised may see it as their only option. Religious believers often show compassion towards people driven to crime by poverty. Jesus taught: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40), encouraging Christians to help the poor rather than simply punish them.

Mental health and addiction: People suffering from mental health problems or addiction may commit crimes because they are not fully in control of their actions. Religious believers may argue that these individuals need treatment and support rather than punishment. Islam teaches compassion for those who are suffering and recognises that people should be judged according to their intentions and circumstances.

Greed and hate: Some crimes are motivated by greed (wanting wealth or power) or hate (prejudice against a group of people). These motivations are generally condemned by religious believers. The Bible warns: “The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10). Islam teaches that greed goes against the principle of zakah — sharing wealth with those in need.

Opposition to unjust laws: Some people break laws they believe are morally wrong — this is called civil disobedience. Rosa Parks broke segregation laws in the USA because she believed they were unjust. Martin Luther King Jr, a Baptist minister, organised peaceful protests against racist laws, arguing that “an unjust law is no law at all” (influenced by St Augustine). Many religious believers support the principle that an immoral law can be legitimately opposed.

Views About People Who Break the Law

Religious believers hold a range of views about lawbreakers. Most agree that breaking the law is wrong, but they differ on how much compassion should be shown and whether the reasons behind the crime matter.

Christians are taught to “hate the sin, love the sinner” — condemning the crime but showing compassion to the criminal. Jesus himself spent time with sinners and outcasts, saying: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick” (Mark 2:17). Islam teaches that humans should show mercy, as Allah is “the most merciful” (Ar-Rahman), but also that justice must be upheld — criminals should face appropriate consequences for their actions.

Key Fact

Religious views on lawbreakers depend heavily on the reason for the crime. Someone stealing bread to feed their starving child may receive more sympathy than someone stealing for greed. Someone opposing an unjust law (like Rosa Parks) may be seen as morally right. Both Christianity and Islam balance justice with mercy, teaching that while wrongdoing must have consequences, rehabilitation and forgiveness are also important.

Types of Crime

The exam specification requires knowledge of three specific types of crime and religious views on each.

Hate crimes are offences motivated by hostility towards a person’s identity — their race, religion, sexuality or disability. Both Christianity and Islam condemn hate crimes because they contradict the belief that all humans are created equal by God. The Bible teaches that God “created mankind in his own image” (Genesis 1:27), and the Qur’an states: “We have honoured the children of Adam” (17:70).

Theft is taking what belongs to someone else. It is forbidden by the Ten Commandments (“You shall not steal” — Exodus 20:15) and by the Qur’an. However, some religious believers show compassion towards those who steal out of desperation, while still condemning the act itself.

Murder is the unlawful killing of another person. It is condemned by all religions as a violation of the sanctity of life. The Ten Commandments state: “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). The Qur’an teaches: “Do not take life, which God has made sacred” (6:151).

title: Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty
content_html:
The Aims of Punishment

When someone breaks the law, society must decide how to respond. Punishment serves several purposes, and religious believers often disagree about which aim should be prioritised. The three main aims studied in GCSE Religious Studies are retribution, deterrence and reformation.

Retribution means making the criminal “pay” for what they have done. It is based on the idea that wrongdoing deserves a proportionate response. The Old Testament teaches “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exodus 21:24), suggesting that punishment should match the severity of the crime. In Islam, the Qur’an also permits retribution: “We ordained for them: a life for a life, an eye for an eye” (5:45).

Deterrence aims to discourage crime by showing the consequences of breaking the law. If people see that criminals are punished severely, they may be less likely to commit crimes themselves. Both Christianity and Islam support the idea that clear consequences help maintain social order, though they disagree about how harsh those consequences should be.

Key Fact

Reformation focuses on helping criminals change their behaviour and become productive members of society. Many Christians prioritise reformation, following Jesus’s teaching about forgiveness and second chances. The Parable of the Lost Son (Luke 15:11–32) shows God welcoming back those who have strayed, suggesting that criminals can be redeemed. Islam also supports reformation — the Qur’an teaches: “But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness” (5:39).

The Treatment of Criminals

There are several ways in which criminals can be punished. Each method serves different aims and raises different ethical questions.

Prison removes criminals from society to protect the public, and provides time for reformation through education and rehabilitation programmes. However, critics argue that prisons can be “universities of crime,” where offenders learn new criminal skills. Many religious organisations, including Prison Fellowship (a Christian charity), work within prisons to support rehabilitation and spiritual growth.

Corporal punishment means inflicting physical pain on the body — such as caning, flogging or beating. It is banned in the UK but remains legal in some countries. Some Muslims argue that corporal punishment is supported by the Qur’an for certain offences, but others argue that it is outdated and contradicts the principle of mercy. Most Christians oppose corporal punishment, arguing that Jesus taught forgiveness rather than physical retribution.

Community service requires offenders to do unpaid work that benefits the local community. It can serve both deterrence (the offender must give up their time) and reformation (the work may help them develop skills and a sense of responsibility). Many religious believers support community service as a humane alternative to prison, particularly for less serious offences.

The Death Penalty

The death penalty (capital punishment) is the most extreme form of punishment — the state-sanctioned execution of a person convicted of a serious crime. It was abolished in the UK in 1965 but remains legal in many countries, including parts of the USA, China, Iran and Saudi Arabia.

Key Fact

Two key ethical principles apply to the death penalty debate. The principle of utility (utilitarianism) argues that the morality of an action depends on its consequences — if the death penalty deters crime and protects society, it produces the greatest good for the greatest number. The sanctity of life principle argues that all human life is sacred and belongs to God, so no human being has the right to take another’s life, regardless of what they have done.

Arguments for: It acts as the ultimate deterrent — people may be less likely to commit serious crimes if they know they could be executed. It provides retribution — some argue that the most serious crimes (such as serial murder or terrorism) deserve the ultimate punishment. It permanently protects society from the most dangerous criminals. The principle of utility may support it if it saves more lives than it takes.

Arguments against: It violates the sanctity of life — only God has the right to take life. Innocent people may be wrongly convicted and executed, and this cannot be undone. It does not allow for reformation — the criminal can never change or make amends. It reduces the state to the level of the murderer. Evidence suggests that the death penalty does not actually deter crime more effectively than long prison sentences.

Contrasting Beliefs on the Death Penalty and Corporal Punishment

Christianity: Most modern Christian denominations oppose the death penalty. Pope Francis declared in 2018 that the death penalty is “inadmissible” and called for its worldwide abolition. The Church of England also opposes it. Christians argue that Jesus taught forgiveness (“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” — Luke 23:34) and that the death penalty denies the possibility of reformation. However, some Christians point to the Old Testament, which prescribed death for certain offences, as evidence that God sometimes sanctions extreme punishment.

Islam: Islamic law (Shari’ah) permits the death penalty for certain serious offences, including murder and apostasy. However, the Qur’an also encourages mercy: “But whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him” (5:45), suggesting that forgiveness is preferred. In practice, many Muslim scholars argue that the conditions for applying the death penalty under Shari’ah are extremely strict and rarely met. Regarding corporal punishment, some forms are prescribed in Islamic law (such as flogging for certain offences), but many modern Muslim scholars argue these should be understood in their historical context.

Key similarity: Both religions teach the sanctity of life and emphasise that mercy and forgiveness are virtues. Both encourage reformation of criminals where possible.

Key difference: Most mainstream Christian denominations now firmly oppose the death penalty, seeing it as incompatible with Jesus’s teachings on forgiveness. Islamic law technically permits it for certain offences, though many Muslim scholars argue that mercy should prevail and that the conditions for its application are extremely difficult to meet in practice.

title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce
content_html:
Human Sexuality

Human sexuality refers to how people experience and express sexual attraction. People may be heterosexual (attracted to the opposite sex), homosexual (attracted to the same sex), or bisexual (attracted to both sexes). In contemporary British society, all three orientations are widely accepted and protected by law.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach that sexual relationships should take place within marriage. However, there is a range of views within Christianity on homosexuality — from conservative opposition to liberal acceptance.

Sexual Relationships Before & Outside Marriage

In modern Britain, sex before marriage is common and widely accepted. However, most religious traditions teach that sexual intimacy belongs within the commitment of marriage.

The Catholic Church teaches that sex must only take place within marriage. St Paul wrote: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). Pope Pius XI declared in 1930 that “every sexual act must be within a framework of marriage.” The Church of England generally agrees but is more lenient towards committed couples. Liberal Protestants tend to accept sex in loving, stable relationships even without marriage.

Islam is clear that sex must only happen within marriage. The Qur’an forbids zinah (unlawful sexual intercourse). Under Shari’ah law, sex before marriage is a serious offence. Abdul Wahid Hamid wrote: “The only way to protect all within society is to maintain a society where only a man and his wife share the act of sex.”

Both Christianity and Islam also condemn adultery. The Ten Commandments state: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14). The Qur’an (17:32) warns: “Do not go anywhere near adultery: it is an outrage, and an evil path.”

The Nature & Purpose of Marriage

Marriage is a formal, legal union between two people. For religious believers, it is more than a legal contract — it is a sacred commitment before God. Christians call marriage a sacrament (Catholics and some Anglicans) or a covenant before God.

Key Fact

The purposes of marriage include: lifelong companionship, a stable environment for children, sexual intimacy within a committed relationship, and (for religious believers) following God’s plan. Genesis 2:24 says a man shall “be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.” The Qur’an (30:21) describes marriage as a source of “love and mercy.”

Same-Sex Marriage & Cohabitation

In a Christian marriage ceremony, couples exchange vows before God, promising to love and cherish each other “for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, till death do us part.” In Islam, the marriage contract is called a nikah. It includes a mahr (financial gift from groom to bride), and both parties must freely consent. The ceremony is often simple, witnessed by family and an imam.

Same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales in 2013. Many liberal Christians support it, arguing that love and commitment matter more than the gender of the partners. However, the Catholic Church and many evangelical Christians oppose same-sex marriage, teaching that marriage is between a man and a woman as God intended.

Islam does not recognise same-sex marriage. Traditional Islamic teaching holds that marriage can only be between a man and a woman, based on the Qur’an’s teachings about the natural order of creation.

Cohabitation (living together without marriage) is increasingly common in Britain. Most Christians prefer marriage but liberal denominations accept cohabitation in committed relationships. Islam does not accept cohabitation because sexual relationships outside marriage are forbidden.

Divorce & Remarriage

Divorce is the legal ending of a marriage. In Britain, divorce is common — roughly 42% of marriages end in divorce. Religious attitudes vary significantly.

The Catholic Church does not allow divorce because marriage is a sacrament. Jesus taught: “What God has joined together, let no one separate” (Mark 10:9). Catholics may obtain an annulment if the marriage was not valid. The Church of England permits divorce and some clergy will remarry divorced people. Most Protestant churches accept divorce as a last resort, showing compassion for those in unhappy or abusive marriages.

Islam permits divorce but discourages it. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Of all the lawful things, divorce is the most hated by Allah.” There is a waiting period called iddah (three months) to allow time for reconciliation and to check if the wife is pregnant. Both men and women can initiate divorce in Islam, and remarriage is permitted after the iddah period.

Key Fact

The ethical tension around divorce centres on two principles: the sanctity of marriage vows (marriage is sacred and permanent) versus compassion (it is cruel to force people to stay in harmful or loveless marriages). Different religious traditions balance these principles differently.

title: Abortion & Euthanasia
content_html:
Sanctity of Life & Quality of Life

Two key concepts underpin religious and ethical debates about abortion and euthanasia. The sanctity of life is the belief that all human life is sacred because it is created by God. Christians point to Genesis 1:27: “God created mankind in his own image.” Muslims believe Allah breathes a soul into every person: “It is He who created you from clay, then determined a term for you” (Qur’an 6:2).

The quality of life is a different concept — it considers whether a person’s life is worth living based on their level of comfort, independence, happiness and freedom from pain. Some people argue that when quality of life is extremely poor, ending suffering may be the most compassionate response.

Key Fact

The tension between sanctity of life and quality of life is at the heart of both the abortion and euthanasia debates. Those who prioritise sanctity argue that life must never be deliberately ended. Those who emphasise quality of life argue that sometimes ending suffering is the most loving and compassionate thing to do.

Abortion

Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy. In England, Scotland and Wales, abortion is legal up to 24 weeks under the Abortion Act 1967 (amended 1990), provided two doctors agree that continuing the pregnancy poses a risk to the physical or mental health of the mother or existing children. After 24 weeks, abortion is only permitted if the mother’s life is at risk or the foetus has a severe abnormality.

Catholic Church: Abortion is always wrong because life begins at conception and is sacred. The Catechism states: “Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception.” The only exception is if a medical procedure to save the mother’s life indirectly causes the death of the foetus (the principle of double effect).

Church of England: Abortion is generally opposed but accepted in certain circumstances, such as when the mother’s life is at risk, in cases of severe foetal abnormality, or after rape. The decision should be made with compassion and careful thought.

Liberal Christians: Some argue that the most loving thing may be to allow abortion in difficult circumstances. They apply Jesus’s teaching of compassion and the principle of “the lesser of two evils.”

Most Muslim scholars oppose abortion after ensoulment (when the soul enters the body), traditionally believed to occur at 120 days. Before this point, some scholars permit abortion in certain circumstances, such as when the mother’s life is in danger. The Qur’an (17:31) warns: “Do not kill your children for fear of poverty.”

If the mother’s life is at risk, most scholars agree that her life takes priority because she has existing responsibilities and relationships. However, abortion for convenience or non-medical reasons is generally considered haram.

Euthanasia

Euthanasia means deliberately ending someone’s life to relieve suffering. It is sometimes called “mercy killing.” There are different types: voluntary euthanasia (the person requests it), non-voluntary euthanasia (the person cannot give consent, e.g. in a coma), and assisted suicide (helping someone end their own life). All forms of euthanasia and assisted suicide are illegal in the UK.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam oppose euthanasia. Christians believe life is a gift from God and only God should decide when it ends. Job 1:21 says: “The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away.” Islam teaches that only Allah determines the time of death: “No soul can die except by Allah’s leave” (Qur’an 3:145). However, both religions support palliative care to relieve suffering without hastening death.

Arguments for: People should have the right to choose how and when they die. Forcing someone to live in extreme pain is cruel. Quality of life matters — when there is no hope of recovery, euthanasia may be the most compassionate option. Some argue Jesus’s Golden Rule (“Do to others what you would have them do to you” — Matthew 7:12) supports ending suffering.

Arguments against: Life is sacred and belongs to God — humans do not have the right to end it. Euthanasia could lead to a “slippery slope” where vulnerable people feel pressured to die. Modern palliative care can manage pain effectively. The Qur’an teaches patience in suffering: “Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear” (2:286).

Death & the Afterlife

Religious beliefs about what happens after death influence attitudes towards euthanasia and the value of life.

Christianity: Most Christians believe in an afterlife. The soul continues after death — the righteous go to heaven (eternal life with God) and the unrighteous face judgement. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die” (John 11:25). This belief gives Christians hope and comfort in the face of death.

Islam: Muslims believe in Yawm al-Din (the Day of Judgement), when Allah will resurrect all people and judge their deeds. The righteous will enter Jannah (paradise) and the wicked will be sent to Jahannam (hell). This belief means Muslims see life as a test and believe suffering has a purpose — it builds patience and strengthens faith.

Belief in an afterlife reinforces opposition to euthanasia. If this life is a preparation for eternal life, then cutting it short may have spiritual consequences. Christians may fear that taking one’s own life or assisting death goes against God’s plan. Muslims believe that accepting suffering patiently is rewarded in the afterlife. However, some non-religious people argue that without an afterlife, reducing suffering in this life becomes even more important — supporting the case for euthanasia.

Key Fact

Humanists and atheists, who do not believe in an afterlife, argue that moral decisions should focus on reducing suffering in this life. They may support euthanasia because they believe people have the right to die with dignity. This contrasts with religious views that see suffering as meaningful and life as belonging to God.

title: The Death Penalty
content_html:
What Is the Death Penalty?

The death penalty (also called capital punishment) is when the state executes a person as punishment for a serious crime. It was abolished in the UK in 1965 as a temporary measure and permanently abolished in 1969. Several campaigns have tried to bring it back, but all have failed.

Today, the death penalty is still legal in some countries, including parts of the USA, China, Iran, and Saudi Arabia. Since abolition in the UK, three people have been pardoned after new evidence proved they were innocent — highlighting one of the strongest arguments against capital punishment.

Key Fact

The death penalty was permanently abolished in the UK in 1969. Since then, three people convicted of capital crimes have been pardoned because they were later found to be innocent.

Arguments For and Against the Death Penalty

The death penalty remains one of the most debated topics in ethics and religion. Both sides use strong moral and practical arguments.

Deterrence — The threat of death may stop people from committing the most serious crimes, such as murder. In some Muslim countries, it is used as a deterrent for murder and rape.

Retribution — It gives justice for the victim and their family. Some argue that the most serious crimes deserve the ultimate punishment.

Protection — It is the only way to guarantee that the worst offenders can never reoffend. Life sentences do not always mean life — murderers in the UK walk free after an average of sixteen years.

Cost — Some argue that housing a criminal for their entire life is a waste of resources that could be better spent elsewhere.

Innocent people could be killed — Legal systems can fail. If someone is wrongly executed, the mistake can never be undone.

No chance for reformation — The death penalty removes any possibility that the offender can change and become a better person.

It is inhumane — Keeping someone on death row for years causes severe mental suffering. Many argue this is degrading and cruel.

It does not deter crime — Countries that still use the death penalty still have high rates of serious crime, suggesting it does not actually prevent offending.

It contradicts the law on murder — If killing is wrong, then the state is committing the same act it seeks to punish, making the executor no better than the criminal.

Ethical Arguments: The Principle of Utility and the Sanctity of Life

Two key ethical arguments are used in the death penalty debate. You need to know both for the exam.

Key Fact

The principle of utility says an action is right if it brings the greatest happiness to the greatest number. The sanctity of life says all life is sacred because it was created by God.

The Principle of Utility — If executing a dangerous criminal protects society and brings greater safety to the majority, then the death penalty could be justified. However, if it causes more pain than pleasure (for example, through wrongful executions or the suffering of death row inmates), then it would be wrong. This argument is difficult to evaluate because measuring happiness and suffering is not straightforward.

The Sanctity of Life — This teaching holds that God created all life, so only God has the right to take it away. Executing a criminal is “playing God.” However, some argue that a murderer has committed such a serious sin against the sanctity of life that they have forfeited their own right to life.

Christian Views on the Death Penalty

Christians hold a range of views on capital punishment. Most modern Christians oppose it, but some find support for it in the Bible.

Most Christians believe only God has the right to take life. The Ten Commandments teach “Do not kill” (Exodus 20:13). Jesus taught forgiveness and warned against judging others harshly. In John 8, Jesus stopped a woman from being put to death for adultery, telling her to “leave your life of sin.” This shows that people should be encouraged to change rather than be executed.

The prophet Ezekiel wrote: “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn away from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11). This supports reformation over retribution. Punishment should help offenders repent and seek forgiveness, which execution makes impossible.

Some Christians refer to Old Testament teachings that appear to support the death penalty. Genesis states: “Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed” (Genesis 9:6). Exodus also teaches “life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exodus 21:23–24). These passages suggest that the death penalty is a just punishment for murder.

Some Christian countries and US states still practise the death penalty. Supporters argue it acts as a deterrent that protects society and allows justice to be seen to be done.

Muslim Views on the Death Penalty

Islam has a complex relationship with capital punishment. Shari’ah law permits the death penalty for certain serious offences, but mercy is also highly valued.

Key Fact

Under Shari’ah law, the death penalty is a hudud punishment for some crimes, meaning the Qur’an says it is compulsory. However, mercy is greatly valued — the victim’s family can accept “blood money” (financial compensation) instead of execution.

The Qur’an teaches: “Do not take life, which Allah has made sacred, except by right” (Surah 17:33). This means life is sacred, but there are circumstances where taking it is permitted. The Qur’an also states: “If anyone is killed unjustly, we have granted the right of retribution to his heir” (Surah 17:33). This allows the victim’s family a role in the punishment.

In practice, public executions are carried out in some Muslim countries to deter others from committing the same crimes. However, many modern Muslims believe the death penalty is outdated, inhumane, and not applied fairly. Organisations like the Muslim Peace Fellowship actively oppose capital punishment.

Case Studies: Derek Bentley and Ruth Ellis

Two famous UK cases highlight the problems with the death penalty. Derek Bentley was executed in 1953 for a murder he did not personally commit — his accomplice fired the gun. Bentley was later given a posthumous pardon in 1998. Ruth Ellis was the last woman to be executed in the UK in 1955. Both cases fuelled public demand for abolition and showed how irreversible the death penalty is when mistakes are made.

title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality
content_html:
The Nature of Families

A family is a group of people connected by blood, marriage or adoption. Families come in many forms in modern Britain. A nuclear family consists of two parents and their children. An extended family includes grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Other family types include single-parent families, blended (step) families, and same-sex parent families.

Both Christianity and Islam place great importance on family life. Families are seen as the foundation of society and the place where children learn right from wrong, receive love and security, and are raised in a faith. In Christianity, the Holy Family (Jesus, Mary and Joseph) is often presented as a model for family life. In Islam, the family is considered the cornerstone of the ummah and maintaining strong family ties is a religious duty.

Key Fact

The role of parents is to provide for their children physically, emotionally and spiritually. The role of children is to respect and obey their parents. The Bible says: “Honour your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12). The Qur’an teaches: “Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be kind to parents” (17:23).

The Purpose of Families

Religious teachings identify several key purposes of family life:

Procreation — Both Christianity and Islam teach that one purpose of marriage and family is to have children. Genesis 1:28 says: “Be fruitful and increase in number.” In Islam, children are seen as a blessing from Allah.

Stability and protection — Families provide a safe, stable environment where children are protected and nurtured. Christians believe the family unit reflects God’s love. Muslims see the family as the building block of the ummah (Muslim community).

Educating children in a faith — Religious families pass on their beliefs and values to the next generation. Christian parents often have children baptised and take them to church. Muslim parents teach children to pray and read the Qur’an from a young age.

Contemporary Family Issues

In modern Britain, same-sex couples can adopt children or have them through surrogacy or IVF. Some Christians accept same-sex parenting, arguing that a loving, stable home is what matters most. Liberal churches emphasise Jesus’s teaching of unconditional love. However, conservative Christians and the Catholic Church oppose same-sex parenting, believing children should be raised by a mother and a father as God intended. Islam does not accept same-sex parenting because homosexual relationships are considered haram (forbidden).

Polygamy means having more than one spouse. It is illegal in the UK. Christianity teaches that marriage is between one man and one woman. However, Islam permits a man to have up to four wives (Qur’an 4:3), provided he treats each wife equally. In practice, most British Muslims are monogamous. The Qur’an itself acknowledges this is difficult: “You will never be able to be equal between wives, even if it is your ardent desire” (4:129).

The Roles of Men & Women

Traditionally, men and women had distinct roles — men as providers and protectors, women as homemakers and carers. Many religious teachings reflect these traditional roles. St Paul wrote: “Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands” (Ephesians 5:22). In Islam, the Qur’an (4:34) states: “Men are the protectors and maintainers of women.”

Key Fact

However, many modern Christians argue for full equality between men and women. Galatians 3:28 says: “There is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Similarly, the Qur’an (33:35) promises equal spiritual rewards for believing men and women. Many Muslims argue that Islam gave women rights to own property, inherit and divorce centuries before Western law did.

Gender Equality, Prejudice & Discrimination

Gender equality means treating men and women with equal rights and opportunities. Discrimination based on gender is illegal in the UK under the Equality Act 2010.

Examples of gender discrimination in religion include the Catholic Church only allowing men to be priests, and some mosques having separate (sometimes smaller) areas for women. However, many denominations now ordain women — the Church of England has had female priests since 1994 and female bishops since 2015. Many Christians and Muslims actively campaign for gender equality as part of their faith’s commitment to justice.

For equality: Both men and women are created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27). Galatians 3:28 teaches spiritual equality. The Qur’an (33:35) promises equal rewards. Jesus treated women with respect and included them among his followers (e.g. Mary Magdalene).

Against full equality of roles: Some believe God gave men and women different but complementary roles. St Paul said women should not teach or have authority over men (1 Timothy 2:12). In Islam, men are traditionally expected to provide financially while women manage the household, though both roles are valued.

Key Fact

Prejudice means holding unfair opinions about someone based on their gender (or other characteristics). Discrimination is acting on those prejudices. Both Christianity and Islam teach that prejudice is wrong because all people are equal before God.

title: Peace, Justice & Forgiveness
content_html:
The Meaning and Significance of Peace

Peace is more than simply the absence of war. For religious believers, peace refers to a deep sense of harmony — between individuals, communities and nations. Both Christianity and Islam teach that peace is a central goal of human life and that believers have a duty to work towards it.

Christians believe that Jesus taught a message of peace throughout his ministry. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). This teaching shows that God values those who actively work to create peace, not simply those who avoid conflict.

In Islam, one of Allah’s 99 names is As-Salaam, meaning “the source of peace.” Muslims greet each other with “salaam alaikum” — “peace be upon you” — reinforcing the idea that peace is woven into everyday Muslim life. The Qur’an teaches that Allah created humanity to live in peace and harmony.

Key Fact

Christianity: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Islam: One of Allah’s 99 names is As-Salaam (“the source of peace”). Both religions teach that peace is a central value and that believers should work actively to promote it.

Justice, Forgiveness and Reconciliation

Justice means ensuring fairness and upholding what is morally right. Religious believers see justice as a divine quality — God is just, and humans should reflect this in their treatment of others. Christians believe that God commands justice: “Act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). In Islam, the Qur’an repeatedly instructs Muslims to act justly, even towards those they dislike: “Be just; that is nearer to righteousness” (Qur’an 5:8).

Forgiveness is the act of pardoning someone who has done wrong and choosing not to hold resentment. Christianity places forgiveness at the heart of its teaching. Jesus said: “If you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Matthew 6:14). On the cross, Jesus prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

In Islam, Allah is described as “the most merciful” (Ar-Rahman) and “the most forgiving” (Al-Ghaffar). Muslims are encouraged to forgive others because Allah forgives those who forgive. The Qur’an teaches: “Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40).

Key Fact

Reconciliation goes beyond forgiveness — it means restoring a broken relationship and rebuilding trust. While forgiveness is a personal decision, reconciliation requires both sides to work together. Christians see reconciliation as central to their faith: God reconciled humanity to himself through Jesus’s death on the cross (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).

Violence means using physical force to cause harm. Some people use violent protest to try to bring about political or social change — for example, fighting with police, destroying property or setting off explosives. UK law allows peaceful protest but prohibits violent protest.

Christianity teaches non-violence. Jesus instructed his followers: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also” (Matthew 5:39). However, some Christians accept that violence may sometimes be a last resort when all peaceful options have failed. In Islam, violence is generally forbidden, but the Qur’an permits self-defence: “Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms” (Qur’an 22:39).

Terrorism is the use of violence against innocent people to create fear and force political change. It is condemned by all mainstream religious traditions. Christianity teaches that every human life is sacred (“sanctity of life”), and Islam states: “Do not take life, which God has made sacred” (Qur’an 6:151).

Some extremist groups claim religious justification for terrorism, but the vast majority of religious believers reject this. Malala Yousafzai, a Muslim education activist shot by the Taliban, demonstrated that faith inspires peace, not violence: “With guns you can kill terrorists, with education you can kill terrorism.” Nelson Mandela, a Christian, spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid through protest rather than terrorism.

Contrasting Beliefs on Violence

Christians and Muslims share many views on violence, but there are important differences in emphasis. Most Christians follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” and believe violence should be avoided wherever possible. The Quaker tradition (Society of Friends) takes an absolute pacifist stance, rejecting all forms of violence.

In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle in defence of Islam, but only under strict conditions — it must be declared by a legitimate authority, be proportionate, and be a last resort. The majority of Muslims reject violence as a tool for spreading faith, emphasising that “there is no compulsion in religion” (Qur’an 2:256). The key contrast is that Christianity has a stronger tradition of absolute pacifism (through groups like the Quakers), while Islam more explicitly permits defensive violence under strict conditions — but both religions agree that peace should always be the primary goal.

title: Death and an Afterlife
content_html:
What Happens After We Die?

One of the biggest questions humans have ever asked is what happens after death. Different religions and worldviews give very different answers. For AQA Religious Studies, you need to understand akhirah (the Islamic concept of life after death), Christian beliefs about the afterlife, and how non-religious people respond to the question.

These beliefs are not just abstract ideas — they directly shape how people value human life and make moral decisions while they are alive.

Key Fact

Christians and Muslims believe in heaven (paradise) and hell. Some Christians, such as Catholics, also believe in purgatory. Non-religious people generally do not believe in any afterlife.

Christian Beliefs About the Afterlife

Christians believe that after death, people face judgement from God. Those who have lived according to God’s will are rewarded with eternal life in heaven, while those who have rejected God face eternal separation from him in hell.

There are two main Christian beliefs about how the afterlife works:

Immortality of the soul — Some Christians believe the soul is eternal and continues living immediately after death. Jesus told the thief on the cross: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). This suggests the afterlife begins straight away.

Resurrection of the body — Other Christians believe that the dead will be physically raised at the end of time. Bible verses describe people “rising from their graves,” suggesting a future bodily resurrection on Judgement Day.

Some Christians, including Catholics, believe in both — the soul lives on after death but will be reunited with a resurrected body at the end of time.

Purgatory is a state that some Christians, particularly Catholics, believe people go to after death in order to atone for their sins before they can enter heaven. It is not a permanent destination but a place of purification.

Many Protestant Christians do not believe in purgatory because Jesus does not mention it directly in the Bible. They believe people go straight to heaven or hell after judgement.

Muslim Beliefs About the Afterlife

In Islam, belief in akhirah (life after death) is one of the six articles of faith. Muslims believe that life on earth is a test from Allah. How a person lives determines what happens to them after death.

Key Fact

Muslims believe that after death, the soul enters a state called barzakh — a waiting period between death and the Day of Judgement. During barzakh, the soul remains in the grave and is questioned by angels about its faith and actions.

On the Day of Judgement, all people will be resurrected and brought before Allah. Their deeds will be weighed, and those who have lived righteously will enter Jannah (paradise), while those who have done evil will be sent to Jahannam (hell).

The Qur’an describes Jannah as a place of gardens, rivers, and eternal peace. Jahannam is described as a place of fire and torment. Muslims believe that living a good life — following the Five Pillars, showing compassion, and obeying Allah — is the way to earn a place in paradise.

Non-Religious Views

Non-religious people, such as atheists and humanists, generally do not believe in any form of afterlife. They argue that science can only prove the existence of the physical world, and there is no evidence for a soul or a spiritual realm. When the body dies, consciousness ends.

Some non-religious people find comfort in the idea that a person’s legacy — their impact on others and the world — continues after they die, even without a supernatural afterlife.

Key Fact

Other religions have different views: Hindus, Buddhists, and Sikhs believe in reincarnation — being reborn in a new body after death. Judaism does not have a single fixed concept of the afterlife.

How Beliefs About Death Affect the Value of Life

Beliefs about what happens after death have a direct impact on how people value human life:

Those who do not believe in an afterlife may value human life more, because they see it as the only life a person has. This can motivate people to make the most of their time and treat others well.

Those who believe in an afterlife may value human life because it is sacred and given by God. However, some may focus more on the afterlife than on earthly life. Christians and Muslims know they will be with God in heaven if they act the way he wants them to.

Those who believe in reincarnation may value human life as a means to achieve a better next life through good actions (karma).

For Christians and Muslims, belief in the afterlife reinforces the sanctity of life. Life is valuable because God has given it, and only God should decide when it ends. Muslims believe life is a test — they will be judged on their actions and rewarded or punished accordingly. This belief motivates ethical behaviour and care for others.

title: Weapons of Mass Destruction & Peacemaking
content_html:
Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction

Weapons of mass destruction (WMDs) are weapons that can kill huge numbers of people and cause devastation over a wide area. The three main types are nuclear weapons, biological weapons (using disease) and chemical weapons (using poisonous substances). The use of WMDs is one of the most controversial moral issues in modern warfare.

Nuclear weapons are the most powerful WMDs ever created. The atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 killed over 200,000 people, many of them civilians. The long-term effects included radiation sickness, birth defects and environmental destruction that lasted for decades. Today, several countries possess nuclear arsenals, and the threat of nuclear war remains a global concern.

Key Fact

Nuclear weapons violate several criteria of the just war theory: they cannot be used proportionately (their destructive power is too great), they inevitably target civilians (blast radius is indiscriminate), and their long-term effects (radiation, environmental damage) extend far beyond the battlefield. For these reasons, most religious believers oppose their use.

Nuclear Deterrence

Nuclear deterrence is the idea that possessing nuclear weapons prevents war because no nation would risk attacking a country that could retaliate with nuclear force. This was the basis of the Cold War strategy of “mutually assured destruction” (MAD) — if both sides would be destroyed, neither side would start a war.

Arguments for deterrence: Nuclear weapons have arguably prevented major wars between nuclear powers since 1945. The threat of mutual destruction makes war too costly to consider. Some argue that giving up nuclear weapons unilaterally would leave a country vulnerable to attack or nuclear blackmail.

Arguments against deterrence: The threat to use weapons that would kill millions of civilians is itself immoral. Deterrence relies on the willingness to commit mass murder, which contradicts the sanctity of life. Accidents, miscalculations or rogue states could lead to nuclear war regardless of deterrence. The money spent on nuclear weapons could be used to address poverty and suffering.

Contrasting Beliefs on WMDs

Christianity: Most Christian denominations oppose the use of nuclear weapons. The Catholic Church has called for complete nuclear disarmament, and Pope Francis has stated that even the possession of nuclear weapons is “to be condemned.” Jesus’s teaching to “love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44) and the principle of sanctity of life make the mass killing caused by nuclear weapons incompatible with Christian ethics. However, some Christians support nuclear deterrence as a way of preventing war, arguing that the intention is peace, not destruction.

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that war must be proportionate — “If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate” (Qur’an). Nuclear weapons are inherently disproportionate and indiscriminate, violating this principle. Islam also forbids the killing of innocent civilians, which makes the use of WMDs incompatible with Islamic teachings. However, some Muslim-majority countries possess nuclear weapons, arguing that deterrence protects their people from aggression.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam oppose the use of weapons of mass destruction. The key area of debate is possession for deterrence. Some believers argue that possessing nuclear weapons prevents greater harm; others argue that even the threat of using them is morally wrong because it relies on the willingness to kill millions of innocent people.

Peacemaking and the Work of Individuals

Religious teachings have inspired many individuals and organisations to work for peace. Peacemaking involves actively working to resolve conflicts, support victims and prevent future violence. Both Christianity and Islam teach that believers have a duty to pursue peace.

Desmond Tutu was an Anglican archbishop in South Africa who led the fight against apartheid through peaceful means. Inspired by Jesus’s teachings on love and reconciliation, he chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid ended, helping victims and perpetrators to find a path to forgiveness. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984.

Malala Yousafzai, a Muslim from Pakistan, campaigned for girls’ right to education despite death threats from the Taliban. After being shot in the head in 2012, she continued her work, saying: “With guns you can kill terrorists, with education you can kill terrorism.” Her faith in Allah’s plan sustained her through her recovery. She became the youngest-ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 2014.

Religious Responses to Victims of War

Religious organisations play a vital role in supporting victims of war around the world. They provide humanitarian aid, shelter, medical care, education and emotional support to refugees and displaced people.

Islamic Relief Worldwide was founded in Birmingham, UK, in 1984. Inspired by the Islamic principle of zakah (charitable giving), it provides emergency relief and long-term development support to victims of war and conflict worldwide. In recent years, it has responded to crises in Syria, Yemen, Gaza and Afghanistan, providing food, clean water, medical care and shelter to millions of displaced people.

Islamic Relief’s work is motivated by the Qur’anic teaching: “Whoever saves a life, it is as if he has saved the whole of humanity” (5:32). The organisation works across religious boundaries, helping people of all faiths and none. This reflects the Islamic belief in the universal value of human life and the duty to help those in need, regardless of their background.

Other religious organisations involved in supporting victims of war include Christian Aid, CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development), and the Red Cross (founded on Christian principles of compassion). These organisations demonstrate that religious teachings on peace, justice and compassion are not just theoretical — they inspire practical action to help those suffering from the effects of conflict.

title: Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction
content_html:
What Are Weapons of Mass Destruction?

Weapons of mass destruction (WMD) are weapons that have the power to kill and harm huge numbers of people. They cause large-scale damage to people, infrastructure, and the environment. There are three main types: nuclear, biological, and chemical.

Key Fact

The three types of WMD are: nuclear weapons (use nuclear reactions to devastate huge areas), biological weapons (use living organisms or viruses to cause disease and death), and chemical weapons (use toxic chemicals to burn, poison, or paralyse humans and destroy the environment).

It is impossible to use a weapon of mass destruction only on military targets — there will always be civilian victims. The weapons are controlled from a distance as missiles or bombs, meaning those who launch them do not directly see the destruction they cause. Biological and chemical weapons are illegal under international law, but nuclear weapons remain legal for some countries.

Nuclear Weapons and Nuclear Deterrence

Nuclear weapons use the power of atoms, and sometimes radioactive substances, to achieve massive destruction. The atom bombs dropped on Japan at the end of World War II were so devastating that nuclear weapons have not been used in standard military conflict since.

Some countries keep nuclear weapons as a form of nuclear deterrence. The idea is that if a country has nuclear weapons, no other country will dare attack it because of the fear of devastating retaliation. This could lead to Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD), where both sides would be completely destroyed.

Key Fact

Countries that keep nuclear weapons include the UK (Christian majority), Pakistan (Muslim majority), and possibly Israel (Jewish majority). They argue these weapons keep the world safe through deterrence. However, critics say this is a huge waste of money and increases the risk of terrorists obtaining them.

Arguments for keeping nuclear weapons: They deter war due to fear of consequences. They provide security for countries. In an extreme emergency, they could save more lives overall. Some people who generally oppose nuclear weapons may accept their use to prevent a greater evil. Utilitarians may accept nuclear weapons if they result in more pleasure than pain in the long run.

Arguments against nuclear weapons: They can kill many people, going against the sanctity of life and religious commands not to murder. They will almost certainly kill innocent civilians. Radioactive fallout harms future generations. They damage animals and the environment. They do not give victims any chance to survive. Nuclear accidents and tests can be very damaging. They do not fulfil just war criteria.

Christian Teachings on Nuclear Weapons and WMD

Christians hold a range of views on nuclear weapons and WMD. There are no specific teachings in the Bible about nuclear weapons, as they did not exist in biblical times. Instead, Christians apply broader principles about peace, violence, and the value of human life.

Christians who oppose WMD point to Jesus’s teaching: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). They argue that WMD cause indiscriminate harm to innocent people, which contradicts the command to “love your neighbour as yourself” (Matthew 22:39). Several popes have spoken out against WMD because of the direct harm to people and the environment, and the indirect harm caused by spending money on weapons that could be used to help the poor. The Christian Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament is committed to the permanent elimination of nuclear weapons. Quakers are pacifists and oppose all WMD.

Christians who accept nuclear deterrence argue that the Bible allows violence in some circumstances, such as self-defence. They may see nuclear weapons as a necessary evil to keep the peace and protect innocent lives from aggression. Some Christians believe that keeping nuclear weapons as a deterrent — without intending to use them — is morally acceptable if it prevents greater suffering.

Islamic Teachings on Nuclear Weapons and WMD

Islam teaches that violence should only be used in self-defence and must be proportionate. The Qur’an states: “If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate” (Qur’an 2:194). Many Muslims believe WMD are not approved of by Allah because they go beyond defence and do not give victims a fair chance.

The Prophet Muhammad forbade the killing of innocent civilians during conflict. WMD kill indiscriminately, meaning they cannot distinguish between soldiers and civilians. This makes their use incompatible with Islamic rules of warfare. Muslims also greet each other with “salaam alaikum” (“peace be upon you”), reflecting Islam’s emphasis on peace.

However, some Muslims may argue that nuclear deterrence is acceptable to protect a Muslim country from invasion. Pakistan, a Muslim-majority country, possesses nuclear weapons for this reason. The Qur’an states: “Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms” (Qur’an 22:39). Some interpret this as allowing the possession of powerful weapons for defence, though not their offensive use against civilians.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach the sanctity of life and the importance of protecting innocent people. The key ethical question is whether keeping WMD as a deterrent — without intending to use them — can be justified if it prevents war, or whether their very existence is immoral because of the risk of accidental or deliberate use.

title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life
content_html:
Religious Teachings on the Origin of the Universe

One of the biggest questions humans ask is: how did the universe begin? Religious traditions offer explanations through their sacred texts, while science proposes theories based on evidence. The specification requires you to understand both perspectives and how they relate to each other.

Christianity: The Bible describes God creating the universe in six days and resting on the seventh (Genesis 1). God created light, sky, land, plants, animals and finally humans. Genesis 1:1 states: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” Christians believe God created the universe ex nihilo — out of nothing.

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six periods (yawm). Surah 21:30 says: “The heavens and the earth were joined together, then We split them apart.” Allah is the sole creator of everything. The Qur’an (51:47) also states: “We built the universe with great might, and We are certainly expanding it.”

Key Fact

There are different interpretations of these creation accounts. Literalists (or creationists) believe the Bible/Qur’an describes exactly what happened — God created everything in six literal days. Non-literalists believe the creation stories are metaphorical — the “days” represent long periods of time, and the stories teach that God created, not exactly how.

The Big Bang Theory & Religious Views

The Big Bang theory is the leading scientific explanation for the origin of the universe. It proposes that the universe began around 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense point that rapidly expanded.

Many religious believers see no conflict between the Big Bang and their faith. They argue that God caused the Big Bang. Non-literal Christians point out that the sequence in Genesis (light, sky, land, plants, animals, humans) broadly matches the scientific order of events. The Qur’an’s reference to the heavens and earth being “joined together, then split apart” (21:30) has been interpreted by some Muslims as describing the Big Bang. Science explains how the universe began; religion explains why.

Creationists reject the Big Bang because it contradicts a literal reading of Genesis. They argue that the universe was created in six 24-hour days as the Bible states. Some point out that the Big Bang cannot explain what existed before the explosion or what caused it — suggesting there must be a creator. Young Earth Creationists believe the universe is around 6,000–10,000 years old, based on biblical genealogies.

Origins of Human Life

Christianity: Genesis 2:7 says God “formed a man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.” God then created Eve from Adam’s rib. Christians believe humans are unique because they are made in the “image of God” (imago Dei — Genesis 1:27).

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that Allah created Adam from clay (Surah 15:26): “We created man from sounding clay.” Humans are Allah’s finest creation, appointed as khalifah (stewards or caretakers) of the earth.

Evolution & Religious Views

Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection proposes that life developed gradually over billions of years from simple organisms. Humans share a common ancestor with other primates.

Many Christians accept evolution as the process God used to create life. Pope Francis stated in 2014: “Evolution in nature is not inconsistent with the notion of creation.” They see evolution as God’s method. However, creationists reject evolution because it contradicts the literal Genesis account.

Many Muslims also accept that evolution may explain how species develop, but most believe that Allah directly created Adam as the first human. Human evolution from apes is generally rejected because the Qur’an describes Adam’s special creation from clay.

The Value of the World

Key Fact

Religious believers see the natural world as valuable because God created it. Two key concepts are dominion (authority over creation — Genesis 1:28: “Rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky”) and stewardship (caring for creation responsibly). Most modern Christians emphasise stewardship over dominion.

In Islam, humans are khalifah — caretakers appointed by Allah to look after the earth. The concept of awe and wonder describes the feeling of amazement at the beauty and complexity of the natural world, which many believers see as evidence of God’s creative power. Psalm 19:1 says: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”

Both Christianity and Islam teach that humans have a responsibility to protect the environment. Christians believe they will be held accountable by God for how they have treated creation. Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) called on all people to protect “our common home.” In Islam, wasting natural resources is considered wrong. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Do not waste water even if you are at a running stream.” On the Day of Judgement, Muslims believe they will answer to Allah for how they treated the earth.

title: The Environment & Animal Rights
content_html:
Use & Abuse of the Environment

The environment faces serious threats from human activity. Pollution of air, water and land damages ecosystems and harms human health. Climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, threatens the future of the planet. Religious believers see protecting the environment as a moral duty.

The use of natural resources such as oil, gas, coal, water and timber is essential for modern life. However, many of these resources are finite — they will eventually run out. Religious teachings call on humans to use resources responsibly, not wastefully.

Key Fact

Christians believe in stewardship — caring for creation on God’s behalf. Genesis 2:15 says God placed humans in the Garden of Eden “to work it and take care of it.” Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) described the earth as “our common home” and called for urgent action on climate change and pollution.

Muslims believe humans are khalifah (caretakers) of the earth. The Qur’an (6:165) says: “It is He who has made you successors upon the earth.” Wasting resources is considered wrong. The Prophet Muhammad taught: “Do not waste water even if you are at a running stream.” Muslims believe they will be accountable to Allah on the Day of Judgement for how they treated the environment.

Many religious organisations actively campaign for environmental protection. Christian organisations like A Rocha work on conservation projects worldwide. The Church of England has committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2030. Islamic Relief has environmental programmes addressing deforestation and water pollution. The Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change (2015) urged Muslims to take action based on their role as khalifah. These responses show that religious environmental teaching is not just theoretical — it drives real-world action.

Use & Abuse of Animals

Humans use animals in many ways: for food, clothing, medical research, entertainment and companionship. Religious traditions have varying views on how animals should be treated and whether these uses are morally acceptable.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach that animals are part of God’s creation and should be treated with respect. However, most religious traditions accept that humans have a higher status than animals. Genesis 1:28 gives humans dominion (authority) over animals. The Qur’an says Allah “subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and on the earth” (45:13).

Animal Experimentation

Animal experimentation involves testing medicines, treatments or products on animals. This is one of the AQA “contrasting beliefs” topics — you must be able to explain different religious views.

In favour: Many Christians accept animal experimentation if it is necessary to save human lives or reduce suffering. Humans have dominion over animals (Genesis 1:28) and are uniquely made in God’s image. The Catholic Church teaches that animal experimentation is morally acceptable “if it remains within reasonable limits and contributes to caring for or saving human lives.”

Against: Some Christians, particularly Quakers, oppose animal experimentation because it causes unnecessary suffering. They argue that stewardship means protecting all of God’s creatures. Proverbs 12:10 says: “The righteous care for the needs of their animals.” The RSPCA was founded by an Anglican clergyman, reflecting Christian concern for animal welfare.

In favour (with conditions): Some Muslim scholars permit animal experimentation if it is genuinely necessary for medical advances and there is no alternative. Saving human life is a high priority in Islam: “Whoever saves a life, it is as if he has saved all of humanity” (Qur’an 5:32).

Against: Islam generally opposes unnecessary harm to animals. The Prophet Muhammad said: “If anyone wrongfully kills even a sparrow, he will have to answer for it on the Day of Judgement.” Animals are part of Allah’s creation and deserve compassion. Causing pain for cosmetic testing or trivial purposes is considered haram (forbidden).

The Use of Animals for Food

Both Christianity and Islam allow eating meat, but both have rules about how animals should be treated. Christians have no specific dietary laws (Jesus declared all foods clean in Mark 7:19), though many Christians choose to eat less meat or become vegetarian out of concern for animal welfare and the environment.

Islam requires that meat be halal (permissible). Animals must be slaughtered humanely in the name of Allah, with a sharp knife to minimise suffering. Pork is haram. The Qur’an (5:3) lists forbidden foods. These rules reflect Islam’s teaching that animals should be treated with respect even when used for food.

Key Fact

Non-religious perspectives on animal rights are also important. The philosopher Peter Singer argues that animals have the capacity to suffer and therefore deserve moral consideration. Vegetarians and vegans often argue that it is wrong to use animals for food when plant-based alternatives exist. Animal rights organisations like the RSPCA campaign against factory farming and animal cruelty.

title: Good, Evil & Reasons for Crime
content_html:
Good and Evil Intentions and Actions

Every action has an intention behind it. Religious believers distinguish between good intentions (those that aim to help others and follow God’s will) and evil intentions (those that aim to harm others or defy what is morally right). A key question in ethics is whether a good intention can justify an action that causes suffering.

Christians believe that God gave humans free will — the ability to choose between good and evil. This means humans are morally responsible for their actions. The Bible teaches: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31), suggesting that the world was created good but that humans can choose to act in evil ways.

In Islam, humans are also believed to have free will. Allah created humans as his khalifah (stewards) on earth, responsible for making moral choices. The Qur’an teaches that those who do good will be rewarded on the Day of Judgement, while those who do evil will be held accountable: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it” (Qur’an 99:7–8).

Key Fact

Can it ever be good to cause suffering? Some argue that causing suffering can be justified if it leads to a greater good — for example, a doctor performing painful surgery to save a life, or a parent disciplining a child to teach right from wrong. Others argue that deliberately causing suffering is always wrong because it violates the sanctity of life and human dignity. Christianity teaches “do to others what you would have them do to you” (Matthew 7:12); Islam teaches that Allah is merciful and expects humans to show mercy too.

Reasons for Crime

People commit crimes for many different reasons. Understanding why crime occurs helps society respond appropriately and helps religious believers consider how to balance justice with compassion. the specification identifies four main categories of reasons for crime.

Poverty and upbringing: People living in poverty may steal to feed their families or survive. Those raised in environments where crime is normalised may see it as their only option. Religious believers often show compassion towards people driven to crime by poverty. Jesus taught: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40), encouraging Christians to help the poor rather than simply punish them.

Mental health and addiction: People suffering from mental health problems or addiction may commit crimes because they are not fully in control of their actions. Religious believers may argue that these individuals need treatment and support rather than punishment. Islam teaches compassion for those who are suffering and recognises that people should be judged according to their intentions and circumstances.

Greed and hate: Some crimes are motivated by greed (wanting wealth or power) or hate (prejudice against a group of people). These motivations are generally condemned by religious believers. The Bible warns: “The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10). Islam teaches that greed goes against the principle of zakah — sharing wealth with those in need.

Opposition to unjust laws: Some people break laws they believe are morally wrong — this is called civil disobedience. Rosa Parks broke segregation laws in the USA because she believed they were unjust. Martin Luther King Jr, a Baptist minister, organised peaceful protests against racist laws, arguing that “an unjust law is no law at all” (influenced by St Augustine). Many religious believers support the principle that an immoral law can be legitimately opposed.

Views About People Who Break the Law

Religious believers hold a range of views about lawbreakers. Most agree that breaking the law is wrong, but they differ on how much compassion should be shown and whether the reasons behind the crime matter.

Christians are taught to “hate the sin, love the sinner” — condemning the crime but showing compassion to the criminal. Jesus himself spent time with sinners and outcasts, saying: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick” (Mark 2:17). Islam teaches that humans should show mercy, as Allah is “the most merciful” (Ar-Rahman), but also that justice must be upheld — criminals should face appropriate consequences for their actions.

Key Fact

Religious views on lawbreakers depend heavily on the reason for the crime. Someone stealing bread to feed their starving child may receive more sympathy than someone stealing for greed. Someone opposing an unjust law (like Rosa Parks) may be seen as morally right. Both Christianity and Islam balance justice with mercy, teaching that while wrongdoing must have consequences, rehabilitation and forgiveness are also important.

Types of Crime

The exam specification requires knowledge of three specific types of crime and religious views on each.

Hate crimes are offences motivated by hostility towards a person’s identity — their race, religion, sexuality or disability. Both Christianity and Islam condemn hate crimes because they contradict the belief that all humans are created equal by God. The Bible teaches that God “created mankind in his own image” (Genesis 1:27), and the Qur’an states: “We have honoured the children of Adam” (17:70).

Theft is taking what belongs to someone else. It is forbidden by the Ten Commandments (“You shall not steal” — Exodus 20:15) and by the Qur’an. However, some religious believers show compassion towards those who steal out of desperation, while still condemning the act itself.

Murder is the unlawful killing of another person. It is condemned by all religions as a violation of the sanctity of life. The Ten Commandments state: “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). The Qur’an teaches: “Do not take life, which God has made sacred” (6:151).

title: Families and Contemporary Family Issues
content_html:
The Nature of Families

A family is a group of people who are related by blood, marriage or adoption. In the 21st century, families come in many different forms. Both Christianity and Islam teach that the family is the foundation of a stable society, but they recognise that families look very different today compared to the past.

Key Fact

You are expected to know six types of family: nuclear, extended, single-parent, blended (step), same-sex parent, and polygamous. You must also understand the purpose of families and contemporary issues such as same-sex parenting and polygamy.

Types of Family

There are several types of family that you need to know for the exam. Each has a clear definition that the exam board uses.

A nuclear family is a couple and their children living together as a basic social unit. An extended family goes beyond this by including grandparents, aunts, uncles and other relatives. A single-parent family is one parent raising their children alone, perhaps due to bereavement or the end of a relationship. A blended family (also called a stepfamily) is formed when a divorced or widowed person remarries and brings children from a previous relationship. Same-sex parents are two people of the same gender raising children together, often through adoption or surrogacy. Polygamy is the practice of having more than one spouse at the same time.

The Purpose of Families

Both religious and non-religious people agree that the family serves important purposes in society. Families provide stability, protection and education for children. For religious believers, the family also has a spiritual purpose.

Key Fact

The four key purposes of families on The spec are: procreation, stability and the protection of children, and educating children in a faith.

Procreation means having children. For religious believers, this fulfils God’s command to “be fruitful and increase in number” (Genesis 1:28). The family is seen as the proper place for children to be born and raised.

Families create stability for their members and for society as a whole. They protect children by supplying their basic needs and safeguarding them from harm. The Church of England states: “The family remains the most important grouping human beings have ever developed. Children thrive, grow and develop within love and safeguarding of a family.”

For religious parents, educating children in their faith is a key purpose of family life. Christian parents may baptise their children as a way of committing to raising them in the Christian faith. Muslim parents are expected to teach their children how to pray, keep halal food laws and live according to Islam.

Christian Beliefs About Families

Christians believe the family reflects the family of God and provides the basis for a stable society. Parents have a responsibility to care for their children and raise them in the faith. The Bible teaches: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. ‘Honour your father and mother’” (Ephesians 6:1–2). Parents also have duties: “Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21).

The Bible emphasises providing for your family: “Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). Children are described as “a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him” (Psalm 127:3).

Islamic Beliefs About Families

In Islam, the extended family is the basis of Islamic society and part of God’s plan for human beings. The family shapes the moral values and character of children. The Qur’an teaches respect for parents: “Your Lord has commanded that you should worship none but Him, and that you be kind to your parents” (Qur’an 17:23).

The Hadith teaches that “Heaven is under the feet of the mothers,” showing the high status given to mothers in Islam. Children have a duty to care for their elderly parents with kindness and respect. Muslim parents are expected to love and care for their children, set a good example for them, and bring them up in the faith of Islam. The Hadith states: “Honour your children and perfect their manners.”

In Christianity, parents look after their children, caring for them and teaching them about the faith. Children obey their parents and may look after them when they are old. In Islam, men are traditionally expected to provide for the family while women look after the home and raise the children, though many modern British Muslim families share these duties. Children must show respect and care for their parents in old age — the Qur’an instructs: “Lower your wing in humility towards your parents in kindness” (Qur’an 17:24).

Contemporary Family Issues

Modern society raises several issues about family life that religious believers must respond to.

Key Fact

Same-sex adoption is legal in the UK. Polygamy is not legal in the UK, but polygamous marriages performed outside the UK may be recognised.

If a same-sex couple wish to have children, they will generally adopt or have a child biologically related to one parent through surrogacy or sperm donation. Some traditional Christians disapprove of same-sex parents because they believe the ideal is for children to grow up with a male and female role model. Other Christians say it is more important for children to be in a secure and loving family regardless of the gender of their parents. Muslims generally do not approve of same-sex parenting because Islam considers homosexuality morally wrong and believes children should have both a male and female role model.

Bigamy (marrying someone while still married to another) is a criminal offence in the UK. Polygamy may mean that children have the support of more parent figures, but it can also cause jealousy among spouses and mean children see their parents less if a father has multiple households. Christians generally oppose polygamy, though it is not expressly forbidden in the Bible. In Islam, polygamy is permitted under Shari’ah law — a man may marry up to four wives, provided he treats them all equally. However, many Muslims in Britain do not practise polygamy.

title: Abortion and Euthanasia
content_html:
Abortion

Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy. It remains one of the most debated moral issues in modern society. Before 1967, abortion was illegal in the UK, and women resorted to dangerous “back street” abortions that led to infections, injuries, and deaths.

Key Fact
