Under the 1990 Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act, abortion is legal in the UK up to 24 weeks if two doctors agree that at least one condition applies: the mother’s life is at risk, there is risk to her physical or mental health, there is a significant chance the baby would be born with severe disabilities, or an additional child would affect the wellbeing of existing children.

Christian Views on Abortion

Christians hold a range of views on abortion, but all agree that human life has special value because it is created by God.

The Roman Catholic Church teaches that abortion is always wrong. Catholics believe life begins at conception and that destroying a foetus is equivalent to murder. This is rooted in the sanctity of life — the idea that life is sacred because God created it. The Bible states: “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). Catholics apply this directly to abortion.

The Bible also suggests God has a plan for every life before birth: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart” (Jeremiah 1:5). Psalm 139:13 adds: “For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother’s womb.”

However, other Christians, including many Anglicans and Methodists, believe abortion may be acceptable in certain circumstances. Jesus taught that the most important thing is love (agape), and it may be the most loving action to allow abortion if the mother’s life is at risk or the pregnancy resulted from rape. As Colossians 3:12 says: “Clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, gentleness and patience.”

Pro-life supporters believe the foetus has a right to life from conception and that abortion is morally wrong. They argue adoption is always an alternative. Pro-choice supporters believe a woman should have the right to decide what happens to her own body. They argue that a foetus is not yet a person, especially in early pregnancy, and that forcing a woman to continue an unwanted pregnancy can cause serious harm.

Islamic Views on Abortion

Muslims believe human life is precious because it is given by Allah. The Qur’an teaches: “Do not kill your children for fear of poverty — We shall provide for them and for you — killing them is a great sin” (Qur’an 17:31). This verse is widely used to argue that abortion for financial reasons is haram (forbidden).

A key concept in Islam is ensoulment — the moment when the foetus receives its soul from Allah. Many scholars place this at 120 days after conception. Before ensoulment, some Muslims believe abortion may be permitted if the mother’s life is in danger. After ensoulment, abortion is generally forbidden because the foetus is considered a living being with a soul.

The Qur’an also warns: “If anyone kills a person — unless in retribution for murder or spreading corruption in the land — it is as if he kills all mankind” (Qur’an 5:32). Most Muslims agree that the mother’s life takes priority over the life of the foetus.

Euthanasia

Euthanasia comes from the Greek words eu (good) and thanatos (death), meaning “a good death.” All forms of euthanasia are currently illegal in the UK and treated as murder or manslaughter.

Key Fact

Active euthanasia is taking deliberate action to end a life, such as giving a lethal injection. Passive euthanasia is allowing someone to die by withdrawing or withholding treatment. Voluntary euthanasia is when the patient requests death. Non-voluntary euthanasia is when the patient cannot give consent, for example because they are in a coma.

Tony Bland was 18 when he attended the Hillsborough football stadium in 1989. A crush resulted in 97 deaths and left Tony in a persistent vegetative state (PVS) with irreversible brain damage. Although there was no hope of recovery, he was kept alive through tubes providing food and fluids. In 1993, the hospital and his parents obtained court permission to withdraw treatment. Tony became the first patient in UK legal history to be allowed to die through the withdrawal of life-prolonging treatment. The law did not classify this as passive euthanasia.

In September 2015, the British Parliament rejected plans for a “right to die” law in England and Wales. 118 MPs voted in favour and 330 against allowing terminally ill adults to end their lives with medical supervision. In countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, euthanasia is legal under strict conditions — the patient must request it, their suffering must be unbearable, and two doctors must be consulted.

Christian Views on Euthanasia

Most Christians oppose euthanasia because of the sanctity of life. The Ten Commandments state “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13), and Psalm 139:16 teaches that God has ordained every day of a person’s life. The Salvation Army has stated: “All people deserve compassion and care in suffering and dying. Euthanasia and assisted suicide should not, however, be considered acceptable responses. They undermine human dignity and are morally wrong.”

However, some Christians accept the principle of double effect — where medicine given to relieve pain may shorten life as a side effect. They see this as different from intentional killing because the primary intention is to reduce suffering, not to cause death. Many Christians actively support hospice care and palliative care as compassionate alternatives to euthanasia. Jesus taught “Blessed are the merciful” (Matthew 5:7), and Christians apply this by caring for the dying with dignity.

For: People deserve to die with dignity. If someone’s quality of life is very low, it may be more compassionate to let them die. Everyone should have the right to decide how they die. Against: Someone might recover. It is a “slippery slope” that could lead to abuse. No one should carry the burden of deciding another person’s death. It devalues the sanctity of life. As Dr Gunning warned: “Once you accept killing as a solution to a single problem, you will find tomorrow hundreds of problems for which killing can be seen as a solution.”

Islamic Views on Euthanasia

Islam is firmly opposed to all forms of euthanasia. Muslims believe in predestination — that Allah has planned every person’s life, and to end life prematurely is to interfere with His plan. The Qur’an states: “No soul may die except with God’s permission at a predestined time” (Qur’an 3:145), and “Do not kill each other, for God is merciful to you” (Qur’an 4:29).

Key Fact

Euthanasia is haram in Islam. Muslims believe all life is a gift from Allah and only Allah decides when it ends. Suffering may be a test of faith, and caring for the sick is an opportunity to do good that helps a person gain entry to paradise. Unlike some Christians, most Muslim scholars reject even the principle of double effect.

title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships
content_html:
Contraception & Family Planning

Contraception is the deliberate prevention of pregnancy. In modern Britain, contraception is widely available and accepted as a normal part of family planning. However, religious views on contraception vary significantly.

Key Fact

The Catholic Church is the only major Christian denomination that opposes all artificial contraception. Pope Paul VI’s encyclical Humanae Vitae (1968) taught that every sexual act must be open to the possibility of creating life. Catholics may only use natural family planning (tracking fertility cycles).

Most Protestant denominations, including the Church of England, accept the use of artificial contraception. They argue that responsible family planning allows couples to provide better for the children they do have. The Methodist Church stated that “responsible contraception is a welcome means towards fulfilment in marriage.” Contraception can also help prevent the spread of sexually transmitted infections. Protestants see family planning as a practical way to show love and responsibility.

Islamic views on contraception are divided. Many Muslim scholars accept contraception within marriage, particularly if pregnancy would harm the mother’s health, the family cannot afford more children, or it would protect existing children’s welfare. The Hadith records that some companions of the Prophet practised withdrawal (coitus interruptus) and he did not forbid it. However, some scholars oppose contraception because children are a blessing from Allah and humans should not interfere with God’s will. Methods that are permanent (such as sterilisation) are generally considered haram unless medically necessary.

Sexual Relationships Before Marriage

The specification requires you to explain contrasting beliefs about sexual relationships before marriage. In contemporary British society, pre-marital sex is widely accepted. However, most religious traditions teach that sex should be reserved for marriage.

Christianity: The Catholic Church teaches that sex must only take place within marriage. St Paul wrote: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). However, liberal Protestants tend to accept sex within committed, loving relationships even without marriage.

Islam: Sex before marriage is strictly forbidden. The Qur’an prohibits zinah (unlawful sexual intercourse). Under Shari’ah law, sex outside marriage is a serious offence. There is no liberal/conservative divide on this issue in Islam — the teaching is clear and universal.

Same-Sex Relationships

Same-sex relationships are legally protected in the UK. The Equality Act 2010 makes discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal. Same-sex marriage has been legal in England and Wales since 2013. However, religious views on same-sex relationships vary widely.

Key Fact

AQA requires you to explain contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships with reference to Christianity and at least one other religion. Christianity has a wide range of views, from strong opposition to full acceptance. Islam is more uniformly opposed to same-sex relationships.

Christian Views on Same-Sex Relationships

Conservative Christians oppose same-sex relationships. They cite Leviticus 18:22: “Do not have sexual relations with a man as one does with a woman; that is detestable.” The Catholic Church teaches that homosexual orientation is not sinful, but homosexual acts are. The Catechism states that homosexual people “must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity” but should remain chaste.

Liberal Christians support same-sex relationships. They argue that the Bible must be interpreted in its historical context. Jesus never spoke about homosexuality but taught love for all people. Some denominations, such as the Quakers and United Reformed Church, perform same-sex marriages. They point to Jesus’s commandment: “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31).

The Church of England occupies a middle ground. It welcomes homosexual people and recognises civil partnerships and same-sex marriages performed in civil ceremonies. However, it does not currently allow same-sex marriages to take place in its churches. In 2023, the Church of England voted to allow blessings for same-sex couples but stopped short of allowing full church weddings. This ongoing debate shows how religious organisations can evolve on social issues.

Islamic Views on Same-Sex Relationships

Traditional Islamic teaching opposes all same-sex relationships. The Qur’an (7:80–81) tells the story of the Prophet Lut (Lot), whose people were punished for homosexual behaviour. Homosexual acts are classified as zinah under Shari’ah law.

However, some progressive Muslim organisations in Britain argue for greater acceptance. Groups like the Inclusive Mosque Initiative welcome LGBTQ+ Muslims. Many British Muslims also acknowledge that while they may personally disagree with homosexuality on religious grounds, they respect the laws of the country they live in and oppose discrimination against anyone.

Humanists and atheists generally support same-sex relationships and full equality for LGBTQ+ people. They argue that moral decisions should be based on human rights, happiness and the harm principle — not on ancient religious texts. Since same-sex relationships between consenting adults cause no harm, there is no ethical reason to oppose them. The British Humanist Association actively campaigns for LGBTQ+ rights.

Key Fact

The three contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships required by AQA are: (1) conservative Christians oppose them (Leviticus 18:22), (2) liberal Christians accept them (love is most important), and (3) Islam opposes them (Qur’an 7:80–81, story of Lut). You must be able to explain why each group holds its view.

title: Weapons of Mass Destruction & Peacemaking
content_html:
Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction

Weapons of mass destruction (WMDs) are weapons that can kill huge numbers of people and cause devastation over a wide area. The three main types are nuclear weapons, biological weapons (using disease) and chemical weapons (using poisonous substances). The use of WMDs is one of the most controversial moral issues in modern warfare.

Nuclear weapons are the most powerful WMDs ever created. The atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 killed over 200,000 people, many of them civilians. The long-term effects included radiation sickness, birth defects and environmental destruction that lasted for decades. Today, several countries possess nuclear arsenals, and the threat of nuclear war remains a global concern.

Key Fact

Nuclear weapons violate several criteria of the just war theory: they cannot be used proportionately (their destructive power is too great), they inevitably target civilians (blast radius is indiscriminate), and their long-term effects (radiation, environmental damage) extend far beyond the battlefield. For these reasons, most religious believers oppose their use.

Nuclear Deterrence

Nuclear deterrence is the idea that possessing nuclear weapons prevents war because no nation would risk attacking a country that could retaliate with nuclear force. This was the basis of the Cold War strategy of “mutually assured destruction” (MAD) — if both sides would be destroyed, neither side would start a war.

Arguments for deterrence: Nuclear weapons have arguably prevented major wars between nuclear powers since 1945. The threat of mutual destruction makes war too costly to consider. Some argue that giving up nuclear weapons unilaterally would leave a country vulnerable to attack or nuclear blackmail.

Arguments against deterrence: The threat to use weapons that would kill millions of civilians is itself immoral. Deterrence relies on the willingness to commit mass murder, which contradicts the sanctity of life. Accidents, miscalculations or rogue states could lead to nuclear war regardless of deterrence. The money spent on nuclear weapons could be used to address poverty and suffering.

Contrasting Beliefs on WMDs

Christianity: Most Christian denominations oppose the use of nuclear weapons. The Catholic Church has called for complete nuclear disarmament, and Pope Francis has stated that even the possession of nuclear weapons is “to be condemned.” Jesus’s teaching to “love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44) and the principle of sanctity of life make the mass killing caused by nuclear weapons incompatible with Christian ethics. However, some Christians support nuclear deterrence as a way of preventing war, arguing that the intention is peace, not destruction.

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that war must be proportionate — “If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate” (Qur’an). Nuclear weapons are inherently disproportionate and indiscriminate, violating this principle. Islam also forbids the killing of innocent civilians, which makes the use of WMDs incompatible with Islamic teachings. However, some Muslim-majority countries possess nuclear weapons, arguing that deterrence protects their people from aggression.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam oppose the use of weapons of mass destruction. The key area of debate is possession for deterrence. Some believers argue that possessing nuclear weapons prevents greater harm; others argue that even the threat of using them is morally wrong because it relies on the willingness to kill millions of innocent people.

Peacemaking and the Work of Individuals

Religious teachings have inspired many individuals and organisations to work for peace. Peacemaking involves actively working to resolve conflicts, support victims and prevent future violence. Both Christianity and Islam teach that believers have a duty to pursue peace.

Desmond Tutu was an Anglican archbishop in South Africa who led the fight against apartheid through peaceful means. Inspired by Jesus’s teachings on love and reconciliation, he chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid ended, helping victims and perpetrators to find a path to forgiveness. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984.

Malala Yousafzai, a Muslim from Pakistan, campaigned for girls’ right to education despite death threats from the Taliban. After being shot in the head in 2012, she continued her work, saying: “With guns you can kill terrorists, with education you can kill terrorism.” Her faith in Allah’s plan sustained her through her recovery. She became the youngest-ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 2014.

Religious Responses to Victims of War

Religious organisations play a vital role in supporting victims of war around the world. They provide humanitarian aid, shelter, medical care, education and emotional support to refugees and displaced people.

Islamic Relief Worldwide was founded in Birmingham, UK, in 1984. Inspired by the Islamic principle of zakah (charitable giving), it provides emergency relief and long-term development support to victims of war and conflict worldwide. In recent years, it has responded to crises in Syria, Yemen, Gaza and Afghanistan, providing food, clean water, medical care and shelter to millions of displaced people.

Islamic Relief’s work is motivated by the Qur’anic teaching: “Whoever saves a life, it is as if he has saved the whole of humanity” (5:32). The organisation works across religious boundaries, helping people of all faiths and none. This reflects the Islamic belief in the universal value of human life and the duty to help those in need, regardless of their background.

Other religious organisations involved in supporting victims of war include Christian Aid, CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development), and the Red Cross (founded on Christian principles of compassion). These organisations demonstrate that religious teachings on peace, justice and compassion are not just theoretical — they inspire practical action to help those suffering from the effects of conflict.

title: Peace, Justice & Forgiveness
content_html:
The Meaning and Significance of Peace

Peace is more than simply the absence of war. For religious believers, peace refers to a deep sense of harmony — between individuals, communities and nations. Both Christianity and Islam teach that peace is a central goal of human life and that believers have a duty to work towards it.

Christians believe that Jesus taught a message of peace throughout his ministry. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). This teaching shows that God values those who actively work to create peace, not simply those who avoid conflict.

In Islam, one of Allah’s 99 names is As-Salaam, meaning “the source of peace.” Muslims greet each other with “salaam alaikum” — “peace be upon you” — reinforcing the idea that peace is woven into everyday Muslim life. The Qur’an teaches that Allah created humanity to live in peace and harmony.

Key Fact

Christianity: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Islam: One of Allah’s 99 names is As-Salaam (“the source of peace”). Both religions teach that peace is a central value and that believers should work actively to promote it.

Justice, Forgiveness and Reconciliation

Justice means ensuring fairness and upholding what is morally right. Religious believers see justice as a divine quality — God is just, and humans should reflect this in their treatment of others. Christians believe that God commands justice: “Act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). In Islam, the Qur’an repeatedly instructs Muslims to act justly, even towards those they dislike: “Be just; that is nearer to righteousness” (Qur’an 5:8).

Forgiveness is the act of pardoning someone who has done wrong and choosing not to hold resentment. Christianity places forgiveness at the heart of its teaching. Jesus said: “If you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Matthew 6:14). On the cross, Jesus prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

In Islam, Allah is described as “the most merciful” (Ar-Rahman) and “the most forgiving” (Al-Ghaffar). Muslims are encouraged to forgive others because Allah forgives those who forgive. The Qur’an teaches: “Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40).

Key Fact

Reconciliation goes beyond forgiveness — it means restoring a broken relationship and rebuilding trust. While forgiveness is a personal decision, reconciliation requires both sides to work together. Christians see reconciliation as central to their faith: God reconciled humanity to himself through Jesus’s death on the cross (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).

Violence means using physical force to cause harm. Some people use violent protest to try to bring about political or social change — for example, fighting with police, destroying property or setting off explosives. UK law allows peaceful protest but prohibits violent protest.

Christianity teaches non-violence. Jesus instructed his followers: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also” (Matthew 5:39). However, some Christians accept that violence may sometimes be a last resort when all peaceful options have failed. In Islam, violence is generally forbidden, but the Qur’an permits self-defence: “Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms” (Qur’an 22:39).

Terrorism is the use of violence against innocent people to create fear and force political change. It is condemned by all mainstream religious traditions. Christianity teaches that every human life is sacred (“sanctity of life”), and Islam states: “Do not take life, which God has made sacred” (Qur’an 6:151).

Some extremist groups claim religious justification for terrorism, but the vast majority of religious believers reject this. Malala Yousafzai, a Muslim education activist shot by the Taliban, demonstrated that faith inspires peace, not violence: “With guns you can kill terrorists, with education you can kill terrorism.” Nelson Mandela, a Christian, spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid through protest rather than terrorism.

Contrasting Beliefs on Violence

Christians and Muslims share many views on violence, but there are important differences in emphasis. Most Christians follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” and believe violence should be avoided wherever possible. The Quaker tradition (Society of Friends) takes an absolute pacifist stance, rejecting all forms of violence.

In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle in defence of Islam, but only under strict conditions — it must be declared by a legitimate authority, be proportionate, and be a last resort. The majority of Muslims reject violence as a tool for spreading faith, emphasising that “there is no compulsion in religion” (Qur’an 2:256). The key contrast is that Christianity has a stronger tradition of absolute pacifism (through groups like the Quakers), while Islam more explicitly permits defensive violence under strict conditions — but both religions agree that peace should always be the primary goal.

title: Peacemaking and Responses to Victims of War
content_html:
What Is Peacemaking?

Peacemaking means actively working to bring about peace and end conflict. It goes beyond simply avoiding violence — it involves negotiation, reconciliation, and practical efforts to address the causes of war. Religious believers often feel a duty to be peacemakers because their faith teaches that peace reflects God’s will for humanity.

Religious people may work for peace between different countries, between people of different religious groups, and between any other conflicting communities. This can involve speaking out about peace, helping with negotiations, giving money to charity, or campaigning for government action.

Key Fact

A peacemaker is a person who works to establish peace. Both Christianity and Islam teach that believers should actively pursue peace rather than simply wait for conflict to end.

Christian Teachings on Peacemaking

Christianity places a strong emphasis on working for peace. Jesus taught his followers to be peacemakers and to love even their enemies. Several key Bible passages support this:

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). This verse from the Sermon on the Mount shows that Jesus considered peacemaking a sign of being close to God. Christians who work for peace believe they are following Jesus’ direct instruction.

“Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Jesus taught that Christians should respond to hostility with love, not more violence. This challenges believers to seek peaceful solutions even when facing aggression.

Pope Francis, the leader of the Catholic Church, has been influenced by Jesus’ teachings about peace and treating others as you would want to be treated. He has helped to negotiate between different conflicting parties, such as helping to reconcile the USA and Cuba. The Church also speaks out about peace and reconciliation, helps with peace negotiations, and gives money to charity to help victims of war.

The Quakers are a Christian group who are committed pacifists. During World War I and World War II, they refused to fight but took peace-making roles instead — acting as mediators between warring nations, serving as medics, cooks, and mechanics, or directly supporting victims of war.

Islamic Teachings on Peacemaking

Islam is fundamentally a religion of peace. The Arabic word “Islam” comes from “salam,” meaning peace or safety. Muslims greet each other with “salaam alaikum,” which means “peace be upon you.” This shows how central the concept of peace is to Islamic life.

The Qur’an instructs Muslims to pursue peace: “Making peace is better” (Surah 2). It also teaches that Muslims must not refuse peace when it is offered: “But if they incline towards peace, you must also incline towards it, and put your trust in God” (Qur’an 8:61).

Key Fact

The Prophet Muhammad said: “We have finished lesser jihad, let us now focus on greater jihad” (Hadith). Greater jihad is the inner spiritual struggle to be a good Muslim, which includes working for peace and justice in the community.

The concept of ummah (the global Muslim community) means that Muslims feel a responsibility to support one another and to work for peace across national borders. Compassion is central to Islam — the Qur’an lists “the Merciful” and “the Compassionate” among the 99 names of Allah.

Who Are the Victims of War?

Victims of war are not only soldiers who fight. War affects families, friends, children, and anyone living in a war zone. Buildings, water sources, land, and animals are also damaged or destroyed. The suffering caused by war can last for generations — people may lose their homes, their livelihoods, and their sense of safety.

War creates many different types of victims. Those who fight may be killed or seriously injured. Families lose loved ones and may be separated. Children grow up in fear and may miss years of education. Civilians in war-torn areas lose access to clean water, food, healthcare, and shelter. Refugees are forced to flee their homes and countries, often with nothing. The land itself suffers — buildings are destroyed, the environment is polluted, and infrastructure is ruined. This suffering can continue long after the fighting stops.

Christian Responses to Victims of War

Christian teachings encourage believers to respond to victims of war with compassion, mercy, and practical help. Jesus taught: “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31), which means showing care and support to those in need. The Golden Rule — “treat others as you would like to be treated” — also motivates Christians to help.

In the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats, Jesus said: “Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). This teaches that people will be judged at the end of time according to whether they have helped others. Those who give food, clothing, and shelter to people in need will go to heaven. Christians therefore try to help victims of war as a direct response to this teaching.

Key Fact

Christians may respond to victims of war by: praying for victims; campaigning for their government to provide support; helping victims directly by giving clothing, food, or shelter; and giving money to charities so that they can help victims directly.

Christian Aid is a charity motivated by Christian values that helps victims of war around the world. It has provided support to people affected by conflicts in Syria and South Sudan, among other places. Christian Aid provides food and water, education, healthcare, clothing, and shelter to those in need. Its work is a practical example of how Christians put Jesus’ teachings into action.

Islamic Responses to Victims of War

Islam teaches Muslims to show mercy and compassion to all people, especially those suffering because of war. Muslims are encouraged to help victims of war through charity and humanitarian aid. The concept of ummah means Muslims believe in supporting fellow human beings as part of the worldwide Muslim community, regardless of nationality.

The Prophet Muhammad set an example by caring for prisoners of war and treating them with dignity, showing that even enemies deserve humane treatment. The Qur’an teaches: “Whoever has saved a life, it is as though he has saved the whole of mankind” (Surah 5:32). This powerful verse motivates Muslims to protect and support those whose lives are at risk because of war.

Zakah (charitable giving) is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Muslims are required to give 2.5% of their savings to those in need, which can include victims of war. Many Islamic charities channel zakah funds to provide emergency relief, rebuild communities, and support refugees displaced by conflict.

title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism
content_html:
Reasons for War

War is an armed conflict between two or more sides, usually nations or organised groups. There are many reasons why wars begin, but the three main reasons studied in GCSE Religious Studies are greed, self-defence and retaliation.

Greed drives wars fought for power, territory or resources. Many governments disguise greed as other motivations, but religious believers generally consider greed an unjust reason for war. Self-defence is widely accepted as a legitimate reason for fighting — both Christians and Muslims agree that protecting yourself and others from harm is justified. Retaliation means fighting back as revenge for a previous attack. While it can deter future aggression, religious believers warn that retaliation often creates a cycle of violence.

Just War Theory

The just war theory was developed by Christian thinkers, most notably St Thomas Aquinas in the 13th century, to determine when fighting a war could be morally acceptable. It recognises that while peace is always preferable, there are circumstances where war may be the lesser evil.

Key Fact

The criteria for a just war include: (1) it must be fought for a just cause, such as self-defence; (2) it must be declared by a legitimate authority, such as a government; (3) the intention must be to promote good and overcome evil; (4) war must be a last resort, after all peaceful alternatives have been exhausted; (5) there must be a reasonable chance of success; (6) proportional force must be used — no more violence than is necessary; (7) civilians must not be deliberately targeted.

Most mainstream Christian denominations accept the just war theory. The Catholic Church teaches that governments have a right and duty to defend their citizens, provided the strict conditions of a just war are met. The Church of England also supports the just war approach, arguing that there are times when failing to act would cause greater suffering.

However, Jesus’s own teaching emphasises peace and non-violence. He said: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44) and “All who draw the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). This creates a tension within Christianity between the ideal of peace and the practical reality that war may sometimes be necessary.

Holy War

A holy war is a war fought for a religious cause or believed to be commanded by God. In Christianity, the Crusades (11th–13th centuries) are the most well-known example — European Christians fought to recapture the Holy Land from Muslim control. In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, but only under strict conditions.

For a holy war to be legitimate in Islam, it must be declared by a recognised religious authority, be fought in self-defence (not aggression), use proportionate force, and not target civilians, the elderly, women or children. The Qur’an states: “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not like transgressors” (2:190).

Key Fact

Just war vs holy war: A just war uses moral criteria to decide if a war is acceptable — it does not have to be religious. A holy war is fought specifically for a religious cause. Today, most Christian and Muslim leaders reject the idea of holy war, arguing that religion should not be used to justify violence.

Pacifism

Pacifism is the belief that all violence and war is wrong, regardless of the circumstances. Pacifists argue that conflicts should always be resolved through dialogue, negotiation and peaceful protest.

The strongest pacifist tradition in Christianity comes from the Quakers (Society of Friends), who believe that all war is wrong. They follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” (Matthew 5:39) literally and refuse to fight in any conflict. Many Quakers served as conscientious objectors during the World Wars, working as ambulance drivers or in hospitals instead.

Islam does not have a strong pacifist tradition in the same way. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad himself participated in battles to protect the early Muslim community. However, many Muslims emphasise that Islam means “peace” and that the greater jihad — the internal struggle to be a good Muslim — is more important than any physical conflict.

Religion as a Cause of War

Religion has been cited as a cause of conflict throughout history — from the Crusades to modern-day conflicts in the Middle East. However, many scholars argue that religion is rarely the sole cause of war. Most conflicts involve a complex mix of political, economic and territorial factors, with religion sometimes used to justify violence rather than being its root cause.

Both Christians and Muslims argue that their faith promotes peace, not war. Where religious violence occurs, leaders from both traditions condemn it. Pope Francis has stated that “war is always a defeat for humanity,” and Muslim scholars worldwide have signed declarations condemning violence carried out in the name of Islam.

Christianity: Quakers take an absolute pacifist position, rejecting all violence. Most other Christian denominations accept that war may sometimes be necessary (just war theory) but should always be a last resort. All Christians agree that Jesus taught peace and non-violence as the ideal.

Islam: Most Muslims are not pacifists in the absolute sense. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad fought to protect the Muslim community. However, peace is the preferred state, and the greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) is considered more important than the lesser jihad (armed conflict). Some individual Muslims, such as Abdul Ghaffar Khan, have adopted pacifist positions inspired by their faith.

title: Forgiveness & Corporal Punishment
content_html:
Forgiveness in Religious Teaching

Forgiveness is one of the most important concepts in both Christianity and Islam. It means pardoning someone who has done wrong and choosing not to hold resentment or seek revenge. For religious believers, forgiveness is not just a personal choice — it is a moral duty rooted in sacred teaching.

Christianity places forgiveness at the very centre of its faith. Jesus’s death on the cross is understood as the ultimate act of forgiveness — God forgiving humanity for its sins. Jesus taught his followers to forgive others without limit. When Peter asked “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother when he sins against me? Up to seven times?”, Jesus replied: “I tell you, not seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:21–22). This means forgiveness should be unlimited.

Key Fact

The Lord’s Prayer includes the words: “Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us.” This shows that receiving God’s forgiveness is linked to forgiving others. Christians who refuse to forgive cannot expect God’s forgiveness in return. On the cross, Jesus demonstrated this by praying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

In Islam, Allah is described by many names relating to forgiveness, including Al-Ghaffar (“the All-Forgiving”) and Ar-Rahman (“the Most Merciful”). Muslims are taught that forgiving others brings them closer to Allah. The Qur’an states: “Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40). During the month of Ramadan, Muslims are especially encouraged to seek and grant forgiveness.

Non-religious people also value forgiveness, though for different reasons. Humanists may support forgiveness because it promotes human well-being and reduces suffering. Psychologists have shown that holding onto anger and resentment can damage mental and physical health, while forgiveness can lead to healing and improved relationships.

However, some non-religious people argue that forgiveness is not always appropriate. If a criminal has not shown genuine remorse, forgiveness may seem unjust to the victim. Some argue that justice must come before forgiveness — a criminal should face consequences for their actions before any question of forgiveness arises.

Contrasting Beliefs on Forgiveness

Christianity: Most Christians believe that forgiveness is always possible and that believers have a duty to forgive, even when it is extremely difficult. Jesus forgave those who crucified him, setting the ultimate example. However, some Christians distinguish between forgiveness (which is always required) and reconciliation (which may not always be possible or safe). A victim can forgive their attacker without having to re-establish a relationship with them.

Islam: Muslims are encouraged to forgive, but Islam also recognises the right to justice. The Qur’an offers a choice: “The recompense for an injury is an injury equal thereto; but if a person forgives and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40). This means that while forgiveness is preferred and rewarded by Allah, victims also have the right to seek proportionate justice. Some Muslims argue that forgiving is a sign of spiritual strength, while others believe that justice must be served first.

Key Fact

Key contrast: Christianity teaches that forgiveness is unconditional — believers must forgive, even their worst enemies. Islam teaches that forgiveness is highly valued and rewarded by Allah, but it also permits proportionate justice as a legitimate alternative. Both agree that forgiveness leads to reconciliation and is ultimately better for the individual and society.

The Link Between Forgiveness and Justice

One of the most challenging questions in religious ethics is how forgiveness relates to justice. Can you forgive someone while still insisting they face punishment? Most religious believers would say yes — forgiveness is a personal decision about letting go of anger, while justice is about holding people accountable for their actions.

Christians believe that God is both forgiving and just. While God offers forgiveness to all who repent, there are still consequences for sin. The parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31–46) teaches that people will be judged on their actions. Similarly, in Islam, Allah is both Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) and Al-Adl (the Just) — forgiveness and justice are not contradictory but complementary. A criminal can be forgiven by their victim while still serving a prison sentence, because forgiveness and justice serve different purposes.

Gee Walker: In 2005, Anthony Walker, a Black British teenager, was murdered in a racially motivated attack in Liverpool. His mother, Gee Walker, a devout Christian, publicly forgave her son’s killers. She said: “I can’t hate. I have to forgive them. Unforgiveness makes you a victim, and I refuse to be a victim.” Her forgiveness was inspired by her Christian faith and Jesus’s teaching to forgive others. However, she also supported the killers receiving life sentences — showing that forgiveness and justice can coexist.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (South Africa): After apartheid ended in South Africa, Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). Rather than seeking retribution against those who had committed atrocities, the TRC offered amnesty to perpetrators who fully confessed their crimes. Tutu, inspired by his Christian faith, believed that forgiveness and truth-telling were more powerful than punishment in healing a divided nation. He said: “Without forgiveness, there is no future.”

In 2006, a gunman entered an Amish school in Pennsylvania, USA, and killed five girls before taking his own life. The Amish community, deeply committed to their Christian faith, immediately forgave the killer. Members of the community attended the gunman’s funeral and set up a charitable fund for his family. This remarkable act of forgiveness attracted worldwide attention and demonstrated how deeply some Christians take Jesus’s teaching on unlimited forgiveness.

These real-world examples show that forgiveness is not just a theoretical concept — it has transformative power in practice. However, they also show that forgiveness is extremely difficult, especially when the crime is severe. Religious teaching provides a framework for forgiveness, but the personal cost to victims should never be underestimated.

title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life
content_html:
Religious Teachings on the Origin of the Universe

One of the biggest questions humans ask is: how did the universe begin? Religious traditions offer explanations through their sacred texts, while science proposes theories based on evidence. The specification requires you to understand both perspectives and how they relate to each other.

Christianity: The Bible describes God creating the universe in six days and resting on the seventh (Genesis 1). God created light, sky, land, plants, animals and finally humans. Genesis 1:1 states: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” Christians believe God created the universe ex nihilo — out of nothing.

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six periods (yawm). Surah 21:30 says: “The heavens and the earth were joined together, then We split them apart.” Allah is the sole creator of everything. The Qur’an (51:47) also states: “We built the universe with great might, and We are certainly expanding it.”

Key Fact

There are different interpretations of these creation accounts. Literalists (or creationists) believe the Bible/Qur’an describes exactly what happened — God created everything in six literal days. Non-literalists believe the creation stories are metaphorical — the “days” represent long periods of time, and the stories teach that God created, not exactly how.

The Big Bang Theory & Religious Views

The Big Bang theory is the leading scientific explanation for the origin of the universe. It proposes that the universe began around 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense point that rapidly expanded.

Many religious believers see no conflict between the Big Bang and their faith. They argue that God caused the Big Bang. Non-literal Christians point out that the sequence in Genesis (light, sky, land, plants, animals, humans) broadly matches the scientific order of events. The Qur’an’s reference to the heavens and earth being “joined together, then split apart” (21:30) has been interpreted by some Muslims as describing the Big Bang. Science explains how the universe began; religion explains why.

Creationists reject the Big Bang because it contradicts a literal reading of Genesis. They argue that the universe was created in six 24-hour days as the Bible states. Some point out that the Big Bang cannot explain what existed before the explosion or what caused it — suggesting there must be a creator. Young Earth Creationists believe the universe is around 6,000–10,000 years old, based on biblical genealogies.

Origins of Human Life

Christianity: Genesis 2:7 says God “formed a man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.” God then created Eve from Adam’s rib. Christians believe humans are unique because they are made in the “image of God” (imago Dei — Genesis 1:27).

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that Allah created Adam from clay (Surah 15:26): “We created man from sounding clay.” Humans are Allah’s finest creation, appointed as khalifah (stewards or caretakers) of the earth.

Evolution & Religious Views

Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection proposes that life developed gradually over billions of years from simple organisms. Humans share a common ancestor with other primates.

Many Christians accept evolution as the process God used to create life. Pope Francis stated in 2014: “Evolution in nature is not inconsistent with the notion of creation.” They see evolution as God’s method. However, creationists reject evolution because it contradicts the literal Genesis account.

Many Muslims also accept that evolution may explain how species develop, but most believe that Allah directly created Adam as the first human. Human evolution from apes is generally rejected because the Qur’an describes Adam’s special creation from clay.

The Value of the World

Key Fact

Religious believers see the natural world as valuable because God created it. Two key concepts are dominion (authority over creation — Genesis 1:28: “Rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky”) and stewardship (caring for creation responsibly). Most modern Christians emphasise stewardship over dominion.

In Islam, humans are khalifah — caretakers appointed by Allah to look after the earth. The concept of awe and wonder describes the feeling of amazement at the beauty and complexity of the natural world, which many believers see as evidence of God’s creative power. Psalm 19:1 says: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”

Both Christianity and Islam teach that humans have a responsibility to protect the environment. Christians believe they will be held accountable by God for how they have treated creation. Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) called on all people to protect “our common home.” In Islam, wasting natural resources is considered wrong. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Do not waste water even if you are at a running stream.” On the Day of Judgement, Muslims believe they will answer to Allah for how they treated the earth.

title: Gender Equality, Prejudice and Discrimination
content_html:
Gender Equality in Britain Today

Gender equality means that men and women should be given the same rights and opportunities as each other. Many people in Britain today agree with the idea of gender equality, but there are still many examples where it does not happen. Something that prevents gender equality is gender prejudice, which is often based on sexual stereotyping.

An example of sexual stereotyping is the idea that women are more naturally caring or are the weaker sex, so they should look after the home while men go out to work. Stereotyping can lead to gender discrimination — perhaps by not giving a man a job looking after young children or not employing a woman on a building site.

Key Fact

The Sex Discrimination Act (1975) made gender discrimination illegal in the UK. Despite this, it still occurs — on average women get paid less than men, even when doing the same jobs. Women make up roughly half of the workforce, but men hold a higher proportion of senior positions.

Christian Views on Gender Equality

Christians believe that all people have been created as equals in the image of God. The Bible teaches that men and women are equal in God’s sight: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). God created both male and female in his image: “So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27).

Jesus treated women with respect, welcomed them as disciples, and showed in the story of Mary and Martha that women were capable of things other than domestic tasks. He did not conform to the status quo of his day. Christians have worked with charities to improve the treatment of women worldwide and campaigned for more equal treatment of women and men politically.

Some Christians believe that husbands should be in charge of their wives because of biblical teaching: “Wives, be subject to your husbands as you are to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife just as Christ is the head of the church” (Ephesians 5:22–23). St Paul also wrote: “I permit no woman to teach or to have authority over a man” (1 Timothy 2:12).

Some Christians feel that women should focus on motherhood, because important Christian figures such as Mary are revered because they were mothers. The command “with painful labour you will give birth to children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you” (Genesis 3:16) is also cited, though many see this as reflecting punishment for disobedience rather than God’s original plan.

Key Fact

Most Christians today see marriage as an equal partnership where the different gifts of each person, male and female, strengthen family life. Many Christians also argue that inflammatory Bible and Church teachings about gender roles could be considered out of date, reflecting the position of women at the time the Bible was written rather than God’s will for today.

Women in Christian Leadership

The question of whether women can hold leadership roles in the Church is one of the most visible areas of debate about gender equality in Christianity. Some Christians, particularly Catholics, feel that women should not be ordained as priests because of biblical teaching, because Jesus and his disciples were male, and because it is a long-standing tradition in the Catholic Church.

However, other Christians see this as unfair discrimination. Many churches allow women to become vicars and ministers. The Church of England has allowed women to become bishops since 2014. These Christians argue that if God created men and women as equals, then both should be able to serve in all roles within the Church.

Muslim Views on Gender Equality

Muslims believe that God created all people equal. The Qur’an teaches that men and women were created from a single soul and have the same spiritual nature. Men and women have the same religious and moral responsibilities. Muhammad worked to unite tribes in Madinah into one community (Ummah) under God, with equality and justice for all.

The Qur’an states: “People, We created you all from a single man and a single woman, and made you into races and tribes so that you could recognise one another” (Qur’an 49:13). Muhammad also taught that anyone, man or woman, who does a good deed for God’s sake will be rewarded (Qur’an 16:97). He said: “I command you to be kind to women.”

Many Muslim families place high value on the mother’s role in bringing up children in Islam. Men are expected to provide for their families and make decisions about their general welfare. However, many modern British Muslim families share those duties because often both parents have jobs.

Islamic law recognises the full property rights of women before and after marriage. A married woman may keep her maiden name and is entitled to receive material gifts. She does not need to spend her own money on the household and has the right to full financial support within marriage and during the waiting period of divorce.

Key Fact

In some Muslim countries, women are not given full rights under the law, but Muslims point out this is due to different cultural practices rather than the teachings of the Qur’an. Muslim women in the UK may suffer prejudice for the way they dress, for example wearing the hijab. Research shows Muslim women are 71% more likely to be unemployed than white Christian women with the same education level and language skills.

Challenging Gender Prejudice and Discrimination

Christians who think men and women should have different roles may still see them as equal. They may think it is fair to treat them in different ways if this is God’s will. However, Christians who disagree with different gender roles may see men and women being given different roles as unequal treatment, and they may view this as prejudice and discrimination.

Most Christians think it is wrong to treat people differently in any unfair way because they believe God loves everyone equally. The command to “love one’s neighbour” means that to discriminate is not loving. Many non-religious people also agree that men and women should be treated equally. Humanist principles such as fairness and equal rights support this view. Gender prejudice and discrimination is illegal in the UK.

Many non-religious people agree that men and women should be treated equally, and that gender prejudice and discrimination are wrong. Humanist principles of fairness and equal rights support this. However, some non-religious people may believe men and women should have different roles due to biological differences, or may be influenced by social and cultural standards or personal prejudices.

title: Forgiveness
content_html:
What Is Forgiveness?

Forgiveness involves a person letting go of bad feelings towards someone who has caused them harm or pain. Some people believe they should forgive others, while some do not. In the context of crime and punishment, forgiveness raises a difficult question: can all crimes — even the most serious ones like murder — truly be forgiven?

It is important to understand that forgiveness is not the same as removing punishment. A person can forgive a criminal while still believing that justice must be done and the offender must face the consequences of their actions.

Key Fact

Forgiveness is not a replacement for punishment. It is possible to forgive someone and still believe that justice is served when they are punished.

Christian Teachings on Forgiveness

Forgiveness is a core belief in Christianity. Jesus emphasised it throughout his ministry, teaching that Christians have a duty to forgive others. The Lord’s Prayer instructs Christians to ask God to “forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us.” This means that if Christians do not forgive others, God will not forgive them either.

Jesus taught that there should be no limit to forgiveness. When Peter asked, “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother?” Jesus answered, “Not seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:21–22). The Church interprets this as meaning forgiveness should be unlimited.

Even while being crucified, Jesus demonstrated forgiveness by saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Christians believe they should follow Jesus’s example by forgiving others, no matter how serious the offence.

Jesus taught about only one unforgivable sin — blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Some Christians also believe that ceasing to be a Christian is an unforgivable sin. Apart from this, Christianity teaches that God can forgive any sin if the person is truly sorry and repents.

Key Fact

Jesus died on the cross for the forgiveness of humanity’s sins. Christians believe his sacrifice made it possible for all people to receive God’s forgiveness through faith and repentance.

Islamic Teachings on Forgiveness

In Islam, forgiveness is an important value, but it plays a different role compared to Christianity. There are two categories of forgiveness that Muslims recognise:

Forgiveness from God (Allah): Only Allah can truly forgive sins. Allah will forgive those who are truly sorry and intend to follow the faith properly in the future. One of the 99 Names of Allah is Al-Ghaffar (The Forgiving), showing that mercy and forgiveness are central to Allah’s nature.

Forgiveness from humans: Muslims believe that forgiving others stops evil from growing. The Qur’an teaches, “Let them pardon and forgive. Do you not wish that God should forgive you? God is most forgiving and merciful.” It also states, “Pardon each other’s faults and God will grant you honour.” Allah rewards those who forgive.

Unlike Christianity, forgiveness in Islam is optional — it is encouraged but not compulsory. Under Shari’ah law, some crimes are classified as unforgivable (Hudud crimes), such as adultery and rebellion against the state. However, for crimes against individuals (Al-Jinayaat), such as murder, the victim’s family can choose to show mercy. They may accept compensation (“blood money”) instead of demanding the death penalty. This act of mercy is highly valued in Islam.

Real-Life Case Studies

There are powerful real-life examples of forgiveness in action that demonstrate how religious beliefs shape people’s responses to crime.

On Christmas Eve, 68-year-old Alan Greaves was on his way to church to play the organ for Midnight Mass. Two local men made an unprovoked and brutal attack, leaving him for dead. Three days later, Alan died from his head injuries. His wife Maureen, a committed Christian, prayed for those who committed this crime. She wanted to forgive and stop the destructive anger she was feeling. Maureen sought justice but not revenge — her Christian faith taught her to follow Jesus’s example of forgiveness.

In 2014, the mother of a murder victim in Iran was given the right under Shari’ah law to determine the fate of her son’s killer, who was due to be hanged. The night before the execution, she dreamt of her son telling her to forgive. She took this as a sign from God. When she approached the killer, instead of pushing away the chair, she slapped him across the face and felt her rage vanish. The noose was removed and the killer was sent to prison instead. This demonstrates how Islamic teachings on mercy can influence real decisions about punishment.

Can All Crimes Be Forgiven?

This is a central debate within religious ethics. Christians generally believe that all crimes can be forgiven because God’s love and mercy have no limits. Jesus forgave the criminal on the cross beside him, saying “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), showing that even a dying criminal can receive forgiveness.

Muslims take a more nuanced view. While Allah’s forgiveness is limitless for those who truly repent, human forgiveness is optional. For Hudud crimes (offences against Allah), the fixed punishments cannot be reduced by human forgiveness. For crimes against individuals, the victim or their family has the right — but not the obligation — to forgive.

Key Fact

Forgiveness links closely to the aim of reformation. If the primary goal of punishment is to help offenders change and become law-abiding citizens, then forgiveness supports this process by allowing criminals the opportunity to repent and start again.

title: Families, Gender Roles & Equality
content_html:
The Nature of Families

A family is a group of people connected by blood, marriage or adoption. Families come in many forms in modern Britain. A nuclear family consists of two parents and their children. An extended family includes grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Other family types include single-parent families, blended (step) families, and same-sex parent families.

Both Christianity and Islam place great importance on family life. Families are seen as the foundation of society and the place where children learn right from wrong, receive love and security, and are raised in a faith.

Key Fact

The role of parents is to provide for their children physically, emotionally and spiritually. The role of children is to respect and obey their parents. The Bible says: “Honour your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12). The Qur’an teaches: “Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be kind to parents” (17:23).

The Purpose of Families

Religious teachings identify several key purposes of family life:

Procreation — Both Christianity and Islam teach that one purpose of marriage and family is to have children. Genesis 1:28 says: “Be fruitful and increase in number.” In Islam, children are seen as a blessing from Allah.

Stability and protection — Families provide a safe, stable environment where children are protected and nurtured. Christians believe the family unit reflects God’s love. Muslims see the family as the building block of the ummah (Muslim community).

Educating children in a faith — Religious families pass on their beliefs and values to the next generation. Christian parents often have children baptised and take them to church. Muslim parents teach children to pray and read the Qur’an from a young age.

Contemporary Family Issues

In modern Britain, same-sex couples can adopt children or have them through surrogacy or IVF. Some Christians accept same-sex parenting, arguing that a loving, stable home is what matters most. Liberal churches emphasise Jesus’s teaching of unconditional love. However, conservative Christians and the Catholic Church oppose same-sex parenting, believing children should be raised by a mother and a father as God intended. Islam does not accept same-sex parenting because homosexual relationships are considered haram (forbidden).

Polygamy means having more than one spouse. It is illegal in the UK. Christianity teaches that marriage is between one man and one woman. However, Islam permits a man to have up to four wives (Qur’an 4:3), provided he treats each wife equally. In practice, most British Muslims are monogamous. The Qur’an itself acknowledges this is difficult: “You will never be able to be equal between wives, even if it is your ardent desire” (4:129).

The Roles of Men & Women

Traditionally, men and women had distinct roles — men as providers and protectors, women as homemakers and carers. Many religious teachings reflect these traditional roles. St Paul wrote: “Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands” (Ephesians 5:22). In Islam, the Qur’an (4:34) states: “Men are the protectors and maintainers of women.”

Key Fact

However, many modern Christians argue for full equality between men and women. Galatians 3:28 says: “There is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Similarly, the Qur’an (33:35) promises equal spiritual rewards for believing men and women. Many Muslims argue that Islam gave women rights to own property, inherit and divorce centuries before Western law did.

Gender Equality, Prejudice & Discrimination

Gender equality means treating men and women with equal rights and opportunities. Discrimination based on gender is illegal in the UK under the Equality Act 2010.

Examples of gender discrimination in religion include the Catholic Church only allowing men to be priests, and some mosques having separate (sometimes smaller) areas for women. However, many denominations now ordain women — the Church of England has had female priests since 1994 and female bishops since 2015. Many Christians and Muslims actively campaign for gender equality as part of their faith’s commitment to justice.

For equality: Both men and women are created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27). Galatians 3:28 teaches spiritual equality. The Qur’an (33:35) promises equal rewards. Jesus treated women with respect and included them among his followers (e.g. Mary Magdalene).

Against full equality of roles: Some believe God gave men and women different but complementary roles. St Paul said women should not teach or have authority over men (1 Timothy 2:12). In Islam, men are traditionally expected to provide financially while women manage the household, though both roles are valued.

Key Fact

Prejudice means holding unfair opinions about someone based on their gender (or other characteristics). Discrimination is acting on those prejudices. Both Christianity and Islam teach that prejudice is wrong because all people are equal before God.

title: Forgiveness & Corporal Punishment
content_html:
Forgiveness in Religious Teaching

Forgiveness is one of the most important concepts in both Christianity and Islam. It means pardoning someone who has done wrong and choosing not to hold resentment or seek revenge. For religious believers, forgiveness is not just a personal choice — it is a moral duty rooted in sacred teaching.

Christianity places forgiveness at the very centre of its faith. Jesus’s death on the cross is understood as the ultimate act of forgiveness — God forgiving humanity for its sins. Jesus taught his followers to forgive others without limit. When Peter asked “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother when he sins against me? Up to seven times?”, Jesus replied: “I tell you, not seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:21–22). This means forgiveness should be unlimited.

Key Fact

The Lord’s Prayer includes the words: “Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us.” This shows that receiving God’s forgiveness is linked to forgiving others. Christians who refuse to forgive cannot expect God’s forgiveness in return. On the cross, Jesus demonstrated this by praying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

In Islam, Allah is described by many names relating to forgiveness, including Al-Ghaffar (“the All-Forgiving”) and Ar-Rahman (“the Most Merciful”). Muslims are taught that forgiving others brings them closer to Allah. The Qur’an states: “Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40). During the month of Ramadan, Muslims are especially encouraged to seek and grant forgiveness.

Non-religious people also value forgiveness, though for different reasons. Humanists may support forgiveness because it promotes human well-being and reduces suffering. Psychologists have shown that holding onto anger and resentment can damage mental and physical health, while forgiveness can lead to healing and improved relationships.

However, some non-religious people argue that forgiveness is not always appropriate. If a criminal has not shown genuine remorse, forgiveness may seem unjust to the victim. Some argue that justice must come before forgiveness — a criminal should face consequences for their actions before any question of forgiveness arises.

Contrasting Beliefs on Forgiveness

Christianity: Most Christians believe that forgiveness is always possible and that believers have a duty to forgive, even when it is extremely difficult. Jesus forgave those who crucified him, setting the ultimate example. However, some Christians distinguish between forgiveness (which is always required) and reconciliation (which may not always be possible or safe). A victim can forgive their attacker without having to re-establish a relationship with them.

Islam: Muslims are encouraged to forgive, but Islam also recognises the right to justice. The Qur’an offers a choice: “The recompense for an injury is an injury equal thereto; but if a person forgives and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40). This means that while forgiveness is preferred and rewarded by Allah, victims also have the right to seek proportionate justice. Some Muslims argue that forgiving is a sign of spiritual strength, while others believe that justice must be served first.

Key Fact

Key contrast: Christianity teaches that forgiveness is unconditional — believers must forgive, even their worst enemies. Islam teaches that forgiveness is highly valued and rewarded by Allah, but it also permits proportionate justice as a legitimate alternative. Both agree that forgiveness leads to reconciliation and is ultimately better for the individual and society.

The Link Between Forgiveness and Justice

One of the most challenging questions in religious ethics is how forgiveness relates to justice. Can you forgive someone while still insisting they face punishment? Most religious believers would say yes — forgiveness is a personal decision about letting go of anger, while justice is about holding people accountable for their actions.

Christians believe that God is both forgiving and just. While God offers forgiveness to all who repent, there are still consequences for sin. The parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31–46) teaches that people will be judged on their actions. Similarly, in Islam, Allah is both Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) and Al-Adl (the Just) — forgiveness and justice are not contradictory but complementary. A criminal can be forgiven by their victim while still serving a prison sentence, because forgiveness and justice serve different purposes.

Gee Walker: In 2005, Anthony Walker, a Black British teenager, was murdered in a racially motivated attack in Liverpool. His mother, Gee Walker, a devout Christian, publicly forgave her son’s killers. She said: “I can’t hate. I have to forgive them. Unforgiveness makes you a victim, and I refuse to be a victim.” Her forgiveness was inspired by her Christian faith and Jesus’s teaching to forgive others. However, she also supported the killers receiving life sentences — showing that forgiveness and justice can coexist.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (South Africa): After apartheid ended in South Africa, Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). Rather than seeking retribution against those who had committed atrocities, the TRC offered amnesty to perpetrators who fully confessed their crimes. Tutu, inspired by his Christian faith, believed that forgiveness and truth-telling were more powerful than punishment in healing a divided nation. He said: “Without forgiveness, there is no future.”

In 2006, a gunman entered an Amish school in Pennsylvania, USA, and killed five girls before taking his own life. The Amish community, deeply committed to their Christian faith, immediately forgave the killer. Members of the community attended the gunman’s funeral and set up a charitable fund for his family. This remarkable act of forgiveness attracted worldwide attention and demonstrated how deeply some Christians take Jesus’s teaching on unlimited forgiveness.

These real-world examples show that forgiveness is not just a theoretical concept — it has transformative power in practice. However, they also show that forgiveness is extremely difficult, especially when the crime is severe. Religious teaching provides a framework for forgiveness, but the personal cost to victims should never be underestimated.

title: Contraception & Same-Sex Relationships
content_html:
Contraception & Family Planning

Contraception is the deliberate prevention of pregnancy. In modern Britain, contraception is widely available and accepted as a normal part of family planning. However, religious views on contraception vary significantly.

Key Fact

The Catholic Church is the only major Christian denomination that opposes all artificial contraception. Pope Paul VI’s encyclical Humanae Vitae (1968) taught that every sexual act must be open to the possibility of creating life. Catholics may only use natural family planning (tracking fertility cycles).

Most Protestant denominations, including the Church of England, accept the use of artificial contraception. They argue that responsible family planning allows couples to provide better for the children they do have. The Methodist Church stated that “responsible contraception is a welcome means towards fulfilment in marriage.” Contraception can also help prevent the spread of sexually transmitted infections. Protestants see family planning as a practical way to show love and responsibility.

Islamic views on contraception are divided. Many Muslim scholars accept contraception within marriage, particularly if pregnancy would harm the mother’s health, the family cannot afford more children, or it would protect existing children’s welfare. The Hadith records that some companions of the Prophet practised withdrawal (coitus interruptus) and he did not forbid it. However, some scholars oppose contraception because children are a blessing from Allah and humans should not interfere with God’s will. Methods that are permanent (such as sterilisation) are generally considered haram unless medically necessary.

Sexual Relationships Before Marriage

The specification requires you to explain contrasting beliefs about sexual relationships before marriage. In contemporary British society, pre-marital sex is widely accepted. However, most religious traditions teach that sex should be reserved for marriage.

Christianity: The Catholic Church teaches that sex must only take place within marriage. St Paul wrote: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). However, liberal Protestants tend to accept sex within committed, loving relationships even without marriage.

Islam: Sex before marriage is strictly forbidden. The Qur’an prohibits zinah (unlawful sexual intercourse). Under Shari’ah law, sex outside marriage is a serious offence. There is no liberal/conservative divide on this issue in Islam — the teaching is clear and universal.

Same-Sex Relationships

Same-sex relationships are legally protected in the UK. The Equality Act 2010 makes discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal. Same-sex marriage has been legal in England and Wales since 2013. However, religious views on same-sex relationships vary widely.

Key Fact

AQA requires you to explain contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships with reference to Christianity and at least one other religion. Christianity has a wide range of views, from strong opposition to full acceptance. Islam is more uniformly opposed to same-sex relationships.

Christian Views on Same-Sex Relationships

Conservative Christians oppose same-sex relationships. They cite Leviticus 18:22: “Do not have sexual relations with a man as one does with a woman; that is detestable.” The Catholic Church teaches that homosexual orientation is not sinful, but homosexual acts are. The Catechism states that homosexual people “must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity” but should remain chaste.

Liberal Christians support same-sex relationships. They argue that the Bible must be interpreted in its historical context. Jesus never spoke about homosexuality but taught love for all people. Some denominations, such as the Quakers and United Reformed Church, perform same-sex marriages. They point to Jesus’s commandment: “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31).

The Church of England occupies a middle ground. It welcomes homosexual people and recognises civil partnerships and same-sex marriages performed in civil ceremonies. However, it does not currently allow same-sex marriages to take place in its churches. In 2023, the Church of England voted to allow blessings for same-sex couples but stopped short of allowing full church weddings. This ongoing debate shows how religious organisations can evolve on social issues.

Islamic Views on Same-Sex Relationships

Traditional Islamic teaching opposes all same-sex relationships. The Qur’an (7:80–81) tells the story of the Prophet Lut (Lot), whose people were punished for homosexual behaviour. Homosexual acts are classified as zinah under Shari’ah law.

However, some progressive Muslim organisations in Britain argue for greater acceptance. Groups like the Inclusive Mosque Initiative welcome LGBTQ+ Muslims. Many British Muslims also acknowledge that while they may personally disagree with homosexuality on religious grounds, they respect the laws of the country they live in and oppose discrimination against anyone.

Humanists and atheists generally support same-sex relationships and full equality for LGBTQ+ people. They argue that moral decisions should be based on human rights, happiness and the harm principle — not on ancient religious texts. Since same-sex relationships between consenting adults cause no harm, there is no ethical reason to oppose them. The British Humanist Association actively campaigns for LGBTQ+ rights.

Key Fact

The three contrasting beliefs on same-sex relationships required by AQA are: (1) conservative Christians oppose them (Leviticus 18:22), (2) liberal Christians accept them (love is most important), and (3) Islam opposes them (Qur’an 7:80–81, story of Lut). You must be able to explain why each group holds its view.

title: The Environment & Animal Rights
content_html:
Use & Abuse of the Environment

The environment faces serious threats from human activity. Pollution of air, water and land damages ecosystems and harms human health. Climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, threatens the future of the planet. Religious believers see protecting the environment as a moral duty.

The use of natural resources such as oil, gas, coal, water and timber is essential for modern life. However, many of these resources are finite — they will eventually run out. Religious teachings call on humans to use resources responsibly, not wastefully.

Key Fact

Christians believe in stewardship — caring for creation on God’s behalf. Genesis 2:15 says God placed humans in the Garden of Eden “to work it and take care of it.” Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) described the earth as “our common home” and called for urgent action on climate change and pollution.

Muslims believe humans are khalifah (caretakers) of the earth. The Qur’an (6:165) says: “It is He who has made you successors upon the earth.” Wasting resources is considered wrong. The Prophet Muhammad taught: “Do not waste water even if you are at a running stream.” Muslims believe they will be accountable to Allah on the Day of Judgement for how they treated the environment.

Many religious organisations actively campaign for environmental protection. Christian organisations like A Rocha work on conservation projects worldwide. The Church of England has committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2030. Islamic Relief has environmental programmes addressing deforestation and water pollution. The Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change (2015) urged Muslims to take action based on their role as khalifah.
