These responses show that religious environmental teaching is not just theoretical — it drives real-world action.

Use & Abuse of Animals

Humans use animals in many ways: for food, clothing, medical research, entertainment and companionship. Religious traditions have varying views on how animals should be treated and whether these uses are morally acceptable.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach that animals are part of God’s creation and should be treated with respect. However, most religious traditions accept that humans have a higher status than animals. Genesis 1:28 gives humans dominion (authority) over animals. The Qur’an says Allah “subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and on the earth” (45:13).

Animal Experimentation

Animal experimentation involves testing medicines, treatments or products on animals. This is one of the AQA “contrasting beliefs” topics — you must be able to explain different religious views.

In favour: Many Christians accept animal experimentation if it is necessary to save human lives or reduce suffering. Humans have dominion over animals (Genesis 1:28) and are uniquely made in God’s image. The Catholic Church teaches that animal experimentation is morally acceptable “if it remains within reasonable limits and contributes to caring for or saving human lives.”

Against: Some Christians, particularly Quakers, oppose animal experimentation because it causes unnecessary suffering. They argue that stewardship means protecting all of God’s creatures. Proverbs 12:10 says: “The righteous care for the needs of their animals.” The RSPCA was founded by an Anglican clergyman, reflecting Christian concern for animal welfare.

In favour (with conditions): Some Muslim scholars permit animal experimentation if it is genuinely necessary for medical advances and there is no alternative. Saving human life is a high priority in Islam: “Whoever saves a life, it is as if he has saved all of humanity” (Qur’an 5:32).

Against: Islam generally opposes unnecessary harm to animals. The Prophet Muhammad said: “If anyone wrongfully kills even a sparrow, he will have to answer for it on the Day of Judgement.” Animals are part of Allah’s creation and deserve compassion. Causing pain for cosmetic testing or trivial purposes is considered haram (forbidden).

The Use of Animals for Food

Both Christianity and Islam allow eating meat, but both have rules about how animals should be treated. Christians have no specific dietary laws (Jesus declared all foods clean in Mark 7:19), though many Christians choose to eat less meat or become vegetarian out of concern for animal welfare and the environment.

Islam requires that meat be halal (permissible). Animals must be slaughtered humanely in the name of Allah, with a sharp knife to minimise suffering. Pork is haram. The Qur’an (5:3) lists forbidden foods. These rules reflect Islam’s teaching that animals should be treated with respect even when used for food.

Key Fact

Non-religious perspectives on animal rights are also important. The philosopher Peter Singer argues that animals have the capacity to suffer and therefore deserve moral consideration. Vegetarians and vegans often argue that it is wrong to use animals for food when plant-based alternatives exist. Animal rights organisations like the RSPCA campaign against factory farming and animal cruelty.

title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism
content_html:
Reasons for War

War is an armed conflict between two or more sides, usually nations or organised groups. There are many reasons why wars begin, but the three main reasons studied in GCSE Religious Studies are greed, self-defence and retaliation.

Greed drives wars fought for power, territory or resources. Many governments disguise greed as other motivations, but religious believers generally consider greed an unjust reason for war. Self-defence is widely accepted as a legitimate reason for fighting — both Christians and Muslims agree that protecting yourself and others from harm is justified. Retaliation means fighting back as revenge for a previous attack. While it can deter future aggression, religious believers warn that retaliation often creates a cycle of violence.

Just War Theory

The just war theory was developed by Christian thinkers, most notably St Thomas Aquinas in the 13th century, to determine when fighting a war could be morally acceptable. It recognises that while peace is always preferable, there are circumstances where war may be the lesser evil.

Key Fact

The criteria for a just war include: (1) it must be fought for a just cause, such as self-defence; (2) it must be declared by a legitimate authority, such as a government; (3) the intention must be to promote good and overcome evil; (4) war must be a last resort, after all peaceful alternatives have been exhausted; (5) there must be a reasonable chance of success; (6) proportional force must be used — no more violence than is necessary; (7) civilians must not be deliberately targeted.

Most mainstream Christian denominations accept the just war theory. The Catholic Church teaches that governments have a right and duty to defend their citizens, provided the strict conditions of a just war are met. The Church of England also supports the just war approach, arguing that there are times when failing to act would cause greater suffering.

However, Jesus’s own teaching emphasises peace and non-violence. He said: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44) and “All who draw the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). This creates a tension within Christianity between the ideal of peace and the practical reality that war may sometimes be necessary.

Holy War

A holy war is a war fought for a religious cause or believed to be commanded by God. In Christianity, the Crusades (11th–13th centuries) are the most well-known example — European Christians fought to recapture the Holy Land from Muslim control. In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, but only under strict conditions.

For a holy war to be legitimate in Islam, it must be declared by a recognised religious authority, be fought in self-defence (not aggression), use proportionate force, and not target civilians, the elderly, women or children. The Qur’an states: “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not like transgressors” (2:190).

Key Fact

Just war vs holy war: A just war uses moral criteria to decide if a war is acceptable — it does not have to be religious. A holy war is fought specifically for a religious cause. Today, most Christian and Muslim leaders reject the idea of holy war, arguing that religion should not be used to justify violence.

Pacifism

Pacifism is the belief that all violence and war is wrong, regardless of the circumstances. Pacifists argue that conflicts should always be resolved through dialogue, negotiation and peaceful protest.

The strongest pacifist tradition in Christianity comes from the Quakers (Society of Friends), who believe that all war is wrong. They follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” (Matthew 5:39) literally and refuse to fight in any conflict. Many Quakers served as conscientious objectors during the World Wars, working as ambulance drivers or in hospitals instead.

Islam does not have a strong pacifist tradition in the same way. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad himself participated in battles to protect the early Muslim community. However, many Muslims emphasise that Islam means “peace” and that the greater jihad — the internal struggle to be a good Muslim — is more important than any physical conflict.

Religion as a Cause of War

Religion has been cited as a cause of conflict throughout history — from the Crusades to modern-day conflicts in the Middle East. However, many scholars argue that religion is rarely the sole cause of war. Most conflicts involve a complex mix of political, economic and territorial factors, with religion sometimes used to justify violence rather than being its root cause.

Both Christians and Muslims argue that their faith promotes peace, not war. Where religious violence occurs, leaders from both traditions condemn it. Pope Francis has stated that “war is always a defeat for humanity,” and Muslim scholars worldwide have signed declarations condemning violence carried out in the name of Islam.

Christianity: Quakers take an absolute pacifist position, rejecting all violence. Most other Christian denominations accept that war may sometimes be necessary (just war theory) but should always be a last resort. All Christians agree that Jesus taught peace and non-violence as the ideal.

Islam: Most Muslims are not pacifists in the absolute sense. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad fought to protect the Muslim community. However, peace is the preferred state, and the greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) is considered more important than the lesser jihad (armed conflict). Some individual Muslims, such as Abdul Ghaffar Khan, have adopted pacifist positions inspired by their faith.

title: Abortion & Euthanasia
content_html:
Sanctity of Life & Quality of Life

Two key concepts underpin religious and ethical debates about abortion and euthanasia. The sanctity of life is the belief that all human life is sacred because it is created by God. Christians point to Genesis 1:27: “God created mankind in his own image.” Muslims believe Allah breathes a soul (ruh) into every person at a key stage of foetal development; Qur’an 32:9 describes this in the context of Adam’s creation: “Then He fashioned him and breathed into him of His Spirit.” The dominant Hanafi position places ensoulment at 120 days; some Maliki and Hanbali scholars place it at 40 days. Qur’an 6:2 (“It is He who created you from clay, then determined a term for you”) establishes that lifespan is divinely appointed.

The quality of life is a different concept — it considers whether a person’s life is worth living based on their level of comfort, independence, happiness and freedom from pain. Some people argue that when quality of life is extremely poor, ending suffering may be the most compassionate response.

Key Fact

The tension between sanctity of life and quality of life is at the heart of both the abortion and euthanasia debates. Those who prioritise sanctity argue that life must never be deliberately ended. Those who emphasise quality of life argue that sometimes ending suffering is the most loving and compassionate thing to do.

Abortion

Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy. In England, Scotland and Wales, abortion is legal up to 24 weeks under the Abortion Act 1967 (amended 1990), provided two doctors agree that continuing the pregnancy poses a risk to the physical or mental health of the mother or existing children. After 24 weeks, abortion is only permitted if the mother’s life is at risk or the foetus has a severe abnormality.

Catholic Church: Abortion is always wrong because life begins at conception and is sacred. The Catechism states: “Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception.” The only exception is if a medical procedure to save the mother’s life indirectly causes the death of the foetus (the principle of double effect).

Church of England: Abortion is generally opposed but accepted in certain circumstances, such as when the mother’s life is at risk, in cases of severe foetal abnormality, or after rape. The decision should be made with compassion and careful thought.

Liberal Christians: Some argue that the most loving thing may be to allow abortion in difficult circumstances. They apply Jesus’s teaching of compassion and the principle of “the lesser of two evils.”

Most Muslim scholars oppose abortion after ensoulment (when the soul enters the body), traditionally believed to occur at 120 days. Before this point, some scholars permit abortion in certain circumstances, such as when the mother’s life is in danger. The Qur’an (17:31) warns: “Do not kill your children for fear of poverty.”

If the mother’s life is at risk, most scholars agree that her life takes priority because she has existing responsibilities and relationships. However, abortion for convenience or non-medical reasons is generally considered haram.

Euthanasia

Euthanasia means deliberately ending someone’s life to relieve suffering. It is sometimes called “mercy killing.” There are different types: voluntary euthanasia (the person requests it), non-voluntary euthanasia (the person cannot give consent, e.g. in a coma), and assisted suicide (helping someone end their own life). All forms of euthanasia and assisted suicide are illegal in the UK.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam oppose euthanasia. Christians believe life is a gift from God and only God should decide when it ends. Job 1:21 says: “The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away.” Islam teaches that only Allah determines the time of death: “No soul can die except by Allah’s leave” (Qur’an 3:145). However, both religions support palliative care to relieve suffering without hastening death.

Arguments for: People should have the right to choose how and when they die. Forcing someone to live in extreme pain is cruel. Quality of life matters — when there is no hope of recovery, euthanasia may be the most compassionate option. Some argue Jesus’s Golden Rule (“Do to others what you would have them do to you” — Matthew 7:12) supports ending suffering.

Arguments against: Life is sacred and belongs to God — humans do not have the right to end it. Euthanasia could lead to a “slippery slope” where vulnerable people feel pressured to die. Modern palliative care can manage pain effectively. The Qur’an teaches patience in suffering: “Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear” (2:286).

Death & the Afterlife

Religious beliefs about what happens after death influence attitudes towards euthanasia and the value of life.

Christianity: Most Christians believe in an afterlife. The soul continues after death — the righteous go to heaven (eternal life with God) and the unrighteous face judgement. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die” (John 11:25). This belief gives Christians hope and comfort in the face of death.

Islam: Muslims believe in Yawm al-Din (the Day of Judgement), when Allah will resurrect all people and judge their deeds. The righteous will enter Jannah (paradise) and the wicked will be sent to Jahannam (hell). This belief means Muslims see life as a test and believe suffering has a purpose — it builds patience and strengthens faith.

Belief in an afterlife reinforces opposition to euthanasia. If this life is a preparation for eternal life, then cutting it short may have spiritual consequences. Christians may fear that taking one’s own life or assisting death goes against God’s plan. Muslims believe that accepting suffering patiently is rewarded in the afterlife. However, some non-religious people argue that without an afterlife, reducing suffering in this life becomes even more important — supporting the case for euthanasia.

Key Fact

Humanists and atheists, who do not believe in an afterlife, argue that moral decisions should focus on reducing suffering in this life. They may support euthanasia because they believe people have the right to die with dignity. This contrasts with religious views that see suffering as meaningful and life as belonging to God.

title: Relationships, Marriage & Divorce
content_html:
Human Sexuality

Human sexuality refers to how people experience and express sexual attraction. People may be heterosexual (attracted to the opposite sex), homosexual (attracted to the same sex), or bisexual (attracted to both sexes). In contemporary British society, all three orientations are widely accepted and protected by law.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach that sexual relationships should take place within marriage. However, there is a range of views within Christianity on homosexuality — from conservative opposition to liberal acceptance.

Sexual Relationships Before & Outside Marriage

In modern Britain, sex before marriage is common and widely accepted. However, most religious traditions teach that sexual intimacy belongs within the commitment of marriage.

The Catholic Church teaches that sex must only take place within marriage. St Paul wrote: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). Pope Pius XI declared in 1930 that “every sexual act must be within a framework of marriage.” The Church of England generally agrees but is more lenient towards committed couples. Liberal Protestants tend to accept sex in loving, stable relationships even without marriage.

Islam is clear that sex must only happen within marriage. The Qur’an forbids zinah (unlawful sexual intercourse). Under Shari’ah law, sex before marriage is a serious offence. Abdul Wahid Hamid wrote: “The only way to protect all within society is to maintain a society where only a man and his wife share the act of sex.”

Both Christianity and Islam also condemn adultery. The Ten Commandments state: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14). The Qur’an (17:32) warns: “Do not go anywhere near adultery: it is an outrage, and an evil path.”

The Nature & Purpose of Marriage

Marriage is a formal, legal union between two people. For religious believers, it is more than a legal contract — it is a sacred commitment before God. Christians call marriage a sacrament (Catholics and some Anglicans) or a covenant before God.

Key Fact

The purposes of marriage include: lifelong companionship, a stable environment for children, sexual intimacy within a committed relationship, and (for religious believers) following God’s plan. Genesis 2:24 says a man shall “be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.” The Qur’an (30:21) describes marriage as a source of “love and mercy.”

Same-Sex Marriage & Cohabitation

In a Christian marriage ceremony, couples exchange vows before God, promising to love and cherish each other “for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, till death do us part.” In Islam, the marriage contract is called a nikah. It includes a mahr (financial gift from groom to bride), and both parties must freely consent. The ceremony is often simple, witnessed by family and an imam.

Same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales in 2013. Many liberal Christians support it, arguing that love and commitment matter more than the gender of the partners. However, the Catholic Church and many evangelical Christians oppose same-sex marriage, teaching that marriage is between a man and a woman as God intended.

Islam does not recognise same-sex marriage. Traditional Islamic teaching holds that marriage can only be between a man and a woman, based on the Qur’an’s teachings about the natural order of creation.

Cohabitation (living together without marriage) is increasingly common in Britain. Most Christians prefer marriage but liberal denominations accept cohabitation in committed relationships. Islam does not accept cohabitation because sexual relationships outside marriage are forbidden.

Divorce & Remarriage

Divorce is the legal ending of a marriage. In Britain, divorce is common — roughly 42% of marriages end in divorce. Common reasons include adultery, unreasonable behaviour, growing apart, financial problems and domestic abuse. Religious attitudes to divorce vary significantly, and the question of whether remarriage should be permitted after divorce is closely linked to beliefs about the permanence of marriage vows.

The Catholic Church does not allow divorce because marriage is a sacrament. Jesus taught: “What God has joined together, let no one separate” (Mark 10:9). Catholics may obtain an annulment if the marriage was not valid. The Church of England permits divorce and some clergy will remarry divorced people. Most Protestant churches accept divorce as a last resort, showing compassion for those in unhappy or abusive marriages.

Islam permits divorce but discourages it. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Of all the lawful things, divorce is the most hated by Allah.” There is a waiting period called iddah (three months) to allow time for reconciliation and to check if the wife is pregnant. Both men and women can initiate divorce in Islam, and remarriage is permitted after the iddah period.

Key Fact

The ethical tension around divorce centres on two principles: the sanctity of marriage vows (marriage is sacred and permanent) versus compassion (it is cruel to force people to stay in harmful or loveless marriages). Different religious traditions balance these principles differently.

title: Social Justice and Racial Discrimination
content_html:
What Is Social Justice?

Social justice is the principle that all people in society deserve fair treatment, equal opportunities and access to the resources needed for a dignified life. Religious traditions across the world have produced some of the most sustained arguments for social justice in history — and some of the most powerful social movements for racial equality have been explicitly grounded in religious teaching.

Christian teaching on justice runs through both the Hebrew Bible (Old Testament) and the New Testament. The prophet Amos declared: “Let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream” (Amos 5:24). In the New Testament, Jesus summarised the entire Law as loving God and loving your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22:37–39). Catholic Social Teaching — developed through documents such as Rerum Novarum (1891) and Gaudium et Spes (1965) — explicitly states that every person has a right to work, to fair wages and to conditions of dignity. Gaudium et Spes paragraph 26 states that the social order must be founded on truth, justice, love and freedom.

Key Fact

Key religious foundations for social justice include: Amos 5:24 (the Hebrew prophetic tradition); Galatians 3:28 (Christian equality); the Jewish concept of tzedek (justice) and tikkun olam (healing the world); the Islamic concept of adl (justice); the Sikh teaching of sewa (service as worship); the Hindu virtue of ahimsa (non-harm). Each tradition connects the pursuit of justice to its central understanding of God, human dignity or right living.

Racial Prejudice and Discrimination

Racial discrimination is the unjust or harmful treatment of people because of their race or ethnicity. Religious traditions have both opposed racial discrimination through their teachings and, at times, been used to justify it — a tension that makes the study of religion and race important for understanding history and contemporary society.

Christian teaching on racial equality has been central to some of the most significant social movements of the twentieth century. The civil rights movement in the United States, led in significant part by the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr, drew explicitly on Christian scripture and theology. King, a Baptist minister, used Paul’s letter to the Galatians and the teachings of Jesus on the dignity of all persons to argue for the complete equality of Black Americans. His “Letter from Birmingham Jail” (1963) argued that Christians had a moral duty to resist unjust laws, drawing on the natural-law tradition rooted in Augustine and Aquinas. King’s vision was of a “beloved community” in which the dignity of every person was recognised regardless of race.

In South Africa, the churches played a significant and contested role in the struggle against apartheid. Archbishop Desmond Tutu — an Anglican bishop and theologian — drew on the Christian teaching of imago Dei and the concept of the ubuntu philosophy (“I am because we are”) to argue that apartheid was not only politically wrong but theologically incompatible with Christianity. Nelson Mandela, though his political framework was broader, similarly drew on the language of human dignity. After apartheid ended in 1994, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, co-chaired by Tutu, drew on Christian concepts of confession, forgiveness and reconciliation.

Islam teaches the equality of all people before Allah. The concept of the ummah — the worldwide community of believers — explicitly transcends racial and national lines. The Prophet Muhammad’s final sermon at Mecca stated that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, and no non-Arab superior to an Arab, except through piety. British Muslim organisations including Muslim Aid and the Muslim Council of Britain have made public statements opposing racial discrimination and supporting anti-racist work in Britain.

Jewish teaching on justice is rooted in the concept of tzedek (righteousness and justice) and tikkun olam (“healing the world”). Jewish communities in Britain and the United States were prominent in civil rights movements; many American Jewish organisations supported the civil rights movement alongside Black-led organisations. The Jewish concept of Pikuach Nefesh — that saving a human life overrides almost all other commandments — grounds the principle that every human life has equal infinite value, regardless of background.

Sikh teaching grounds racial equality in the concept of the oneness of humanity expressed through Ik Onkar. Guru Nanak challenged caste-based discrimination in sixteenth-century Punjab, and the langar (community kitchen) at every gurdwara is a practical expression of the teaching that all people are equal. Khalsa Aid, a Sikh humanitarian organisation founded in Britain in 1999, works globally in disaster zones and refugee crises, providing aid regardless of race, religion or background — an expression of the Sikh principle of sewa (selfless service).

Positive Discrimination

Positive discrimination (also called affirmative action) involves giving preferential treatment to members of groups that have historically faced discrimination, with the aim of correcting past injustice and creating greater equality of opportunity. It is a contested policy that raises questions about justice and fairness.

Religious views on positive discrimination vary. Some Christians argue that positive discrimination is consistent with the gospel principle of concern for the vulnerable and marginalised — the “option for the poor” in Catholic Social Teaching, developed in Gaudium et Spes, holds that justice sometimes requires giving particular attention to those who have been most disadvantaged. Other Christians argue that treating people differently because of their race — even to correct past wrongs — conflicts with the principle that all people are equal before God and should be treated as individuals rather than members of a group.

Non-religious ethical arguments also divide on this issue. Those who favour positive discrimination argue from the principle of equality of outcome: if historical discrimination has created structural disadvantage, simply treating everyone “the same” may perpetuate that disadvantage. Those who oppose it argue from the principle of equality of opportunity: people should be judged only on their individual merits, and any policy that judges on group membership may itself be a form of discrimination.

Contemporary Britain provides specific contexts in which religious communities have engaged with questions of racial justice. The Grenfell Tower fire in 2017, in which 72 people died, affected a highly diverse community in west London. Religious communities — including the local mosque, churches and the Notting Hill community — were among the first to respond with practical support. Inquiries into the fire raised questions about how structural inequality, race and poverty intersect in housing policy. The Windrush Scandal, in which British citizens of Caribbean heritage were wrongly detained or deported from 2017 onwards, prompted responses from Church of England bishops and other religious leaders who argued that the dignity of these individuals — many of whom had come to Britain to help rebuild the country after World War Two — demanded immediate redress. These contemporary British examples show how the principles of social justice and racial equality taught by religious traditions continue to be relevant to real events in British life today.

Key Fact

The Reverend Martin Luther King Jr drew on Baptist Christian theology — especially Galatians 3:28 and the concept of the beloved community — in the US civil rights movement. Archbishop Desmond Tutu drew on imago Dei and the ubuntu philosophy in opposing South African apartheid. Both show how religious teaching has directly shaped real-world campaigns for racial justice.

title: Wealth, Poverty and the Uses of Money
content_html:
Religious Attitudes to Wealth

Religious traditions do not uniformly condemn wealth. Most teach that wealth in itself is morally neutral — what matters is how it is acquired, held and used. The concept of stewardship in Christianity holds that everything humans possess ultimately belongs to God, and that humans are responsible for managing these resources on God’s behalf. Genesis 1:28 describes God giving humanity dominion over creation; many Christian theologians interpret this as a duty of care and responsible management, not unlimited exploitation. The Acts of the Apostles (2:44–45) describes the earliest Christian community sharing their possessions: “All the believers were together and had everything in common. They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need.”

Jesus taught extensively about wealth and poverty. His parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21) warns against hoarding wealth without concern for others. The story of Zacchaeus (Luke 19) presents a wealthy tax collector who, on meeting Jesus, gives half his possessions to the poor and repays those he has cheated fourfold — illustrating the transformation that Jesus’s teaching was expected to produce. Catholic Social Teaching, developed through Rerum Novarum (1891) and continued in Laudato Si’ (2015), affirms the right to private property while insisting that wealth carries social obligations and that the needs of the poorest must be met.

Key Fact

Five religious giving duties: Zakat (Islam — obligatory giving, one of the Five Pillars, 2.5% of savings above a threshold); Tzedakah (Judaism — righteous giving or charity, understood as a duty rather than an optional gift); Dasvandh (Sikhism — tithing one tenth of income, contributing to langar and gurdwara community work); Dana (Buddhism — generosity as the first perfection, given to the sangha or those in need); Stewardship (Christianity — using all resources wisely as God’s caretakers, expressed through giving to the poor and tithing).

Islamic Teaching on Wealth and Poverty

Zakat is the third Pillar of Islam: every Muslim who possesses savings above a minimum threshold (the nisab) for a full lunar year must give 2.5% of that wealth to those in need. Zakat is understood not as optional charity but as a religious duty, purifying the remainder of one’s wealth and redistributing resources across the ummah. The Quran states: “And establish prayer and give zakat, and whatever good you put forward for yourselves — you will find it with Allah” (Quran 2:110, paraphrase). In addition to zakat, Muslims are encouraged to give sadaqah (voluntary charitable giving) freely and without expectation of return.

Islamic teaching strictly prohibits riba — the charging of interest or usury. The Quran explicitly forbids riba (Quran 2:275), stating that those who consume interest will arise on the Day of Judgement as those who have been touched by Satan. This prohibition is grounded in the belief that charging interest exploits those in financial difficulty and concentrates wealth unjustly. Islamic finance today operates through structures such as profit-sharing agreements (mudarabah) and leasing arrangements (ijara) that comply with this prohibition. There is debate within Islamic scholarship about the precise definition of riba and how it applies in modern financial systems — with different Sunni and Shi’a scholarly opinions on specific modern financial products.

Tzedakah is the Jewish practice of charitable giving. Crucially, the Hebrew word tzedakah is related to tzedek (justice or righteousness): giving to those in need is understood not as optional generosity but as a matter of justice, because the world’s resources belong ultimately to God and must be shared equitably. The twelfth-century Jewish philosopher Maimonides described a “ladder of tzedakah” ranking different forms of giving from lowest (giving reluctantly and less than one should) to highest (giving someone the means to support themselves independently). The concept of the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25) — in which debts were cancelled and land returned to its original owners — grounds the Jewish tradition’s concern that accumulated wealth should not permanently disadvantage the poor.

Exploitation, Fair Pay and People-Trafficking

Religious teachings on wealth carry specific implications for how wealth is acquired, not just how it is given away. The concept of unfair pay is condemned across traditions. Catholic Social Teaching, drawing on Rerum Novarum (1891), explicitly stated that workers have a right to a wage sufficient to support themselves and their families in dignity. Gaudium et Spes (1965) affirmed the right of all workers to just and equitable remuneration. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly commands fair treatment of workers: “Do not take advantage of a hired worker who is poor and needy... Pay them their wages each day before sunset” (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Sikh teaching condemns exploitation through the principle of honest living (kirat karna — earning one’s livelihood through honest work).

People-trafficking is among the most serious forms of exploitation condemned by religious traditions. It treats human beings as commodities and strips them of freedom, dignity and autonomy. Christian organisations including the Salvation Army and the Catholic Church’s Caritas network have been active in anti-trafficking work in Britain and globally. Islamic teaching grounds opposition to people-trafficking in the principle of human dignity (karama) and the prohibition on enslaving free people. Jewish teaching grounds it in Pikuach Nefesh — the duty to save human life — and in the memory of the Exodus from slavery in Egypt, which is central to Jewish identity.

Buddhist teaching holds that attachment to wealth is one of the causes of suffering (dukkha). The Three Poisons include greed (lobha) as a root cause of unsatisfactory living. The Buddha taught the Middle Way — avoiding both extreme asceticism and excessive indulgence — and monks in the Theravada tradition own very little, relying on the lay community for material support through dana (giving). Lay Buddhists are encouraged to give generously, to avoid livelihoods that involve harming others (covered in the Right Livelihood limb of the Eightfold Path), and to hold wealth without clinging to it.

Sikh teaching describes dasvandh — the giving of one tenth of one’s income to the community. This resources the langar (community kitchen), the gurdwara and charitable work. Khalsa Aid, founded in Britain, embodies dasvandh in practice by providing humanitarian aid globally without regard for race, religion or background. The Sikh principle of vand chhakna — sharing what one has with others — sits alongside dasvandh as an expression of the teaching that wealth is given by God and must be shared.

The Role of Charity and UK Organisations

Religious organisations have founded some of the most prominent international development charities operating in Britain and globally. Christian Aid, founded in 1945, works in over 30 countries addressing poverty and injustice; it draws on the Christian principle of loving your neighbour globally, citing Luke 10:25–37 (the Good Samaritan parable). Islamic Relief, founded in Birmingham in 1984, channels zakat and sadaqah from British Muslim communities to emergency relief and long-term development worldwide. World Jewish Relief, which traces its origins to 1933 when it helped Jews fleeing Nazi Germany, now works with vulnerable communities across the world. Khalsa Aid, founded in Britain in 1999, channels Sikh sewa and dasvandh into disaster relief and refugee support globally.

Religious traditions also raise questions about the nature of charity itself. Jewish tzedakah teaches that the highest form of giving enables independence rather than dependence. Buddhist teaching questions whether charity that does not address the structural causes of poverty is sufficient. Catholic Social Teaching distinguishes between immediate relief work and structural justice — the need to change the conditions that cause poverty, not merely to address its effects. This debate — between charitable giving as relief versus advocacy for structural change — is itself grounded in religious teaching and is a productive area for 12-mark evaluation questions.

Key Fact

Christian Aid (Christian — love your neighbour, Luke 10); Islamic Relief (Muslim — zakat and sadaqah, founded Birmingham 1984); World Jewish Relief (Jewish — tzedakah, origins 1933); Khalsa Aid (Sikh — sewa and dasvandh, founded Britain 1999). Each organisation translates its tradition’s teaching on wealth and poverty into direct action.

title: Human Rights, Equality and Freedom of Religion
content_html:
Human Rights: A Shared Foundation

In 1948, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR). Its Article 1 states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Article 18 protects freedom of religion or belief, including the freedom to change religion and to express belief in practice. Religious traditions across the world both shaped and responded to the UDHR — and their teachings on human dignity provide a foundation for much of what is now called human rights thinking.

Key Fact

The UDHR (1948) Article 18 protects freedom of religion or belief. Religious traditions ground human dignity in different ways: Christian teaching cites Genesis 1:27 (humans created in God’s image); Sikhism teaches the complete equality of all through Ik Onkar (“There is one God”); Islam emphasises the dignity God conferred on all humans (Quran 17:70).

Prejudice and Discrimination

Prejudice means forming a negative view of someone without just cause. Discrimination is when prejudice leads to unequal treatment. Religious traditions offer a range of responses to prejudice. Christian teaching holds that all people are made in the image of God — imago Dei — from Genesis 1:27: “God created mankind in his own image.” This teaching is used by many Christians to oppose discrimination in any form. Paul’s letter to the Galatians (3:28) states: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” This verse is frequently cited in Christian arguments against racial, gender or social discrimination.

Sikh teaching affirms the complete equality of all human beings. The Mool Mantra (Guru Granth Sahib 1a) opens with Ik Onkar — “There is one God” — from which Sikh teaching derives the oneness of all humanity. Guru Nanak challenged the caste-based prejudice of his era by sitting and eating with people of all social backgrounds, and the langar (community kitchen) at every gurdwara remains a living expression of that principle today. Muslim teaching holds that all people are created equal by Allah; the Prophet Muhammad’s final sermon, delivered at Mecca, is often cited for its teaching that “no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, and no non-Arab is superior to an Arab, except by piety and good action.”

The Status and Treatment of Women in Religion

The spec asks students to understand the status and treatment of women in religion — a topic on which different sub-traditions hold significantly different positions. It is important to present each tradition’s actual teaching rather than treating any religion as a single, uniform voice.

Within Christianity, views on women’s roles differ by denomination. The Roman Catholic Church does not ordain women as priests; this position is rooted in the teaching that the priest acts in persona Christi (in the person of Christ). The Church of England, by contrast, voted to ordain women as priests in 1994 and as bishops in 2014. Many evangelical and charismatic Protestant churches ordain women in leadership, while others — drawing on passages such as 1 Timothy 2:12 — restrict certain leadership roles. Quaker (Religious Society of Friends) communities have historically affirmed the equal spiritual authority of women and men since the seventeenth century.

Within Judaism, positions also differ significantly between sub-traditions. Orthodox Judaism does not ordain women as rabbis and maintains a traditional distinction between men’s and women’s roles in worship and communal life. Reform Judaism ordained its first female rabbi in 1972, and Liberal Judaism has done so since 1975. In both Reform and Liberal congregations, women participate fully in all aspects of worship. Contemporary Masorti (Conservative) Judaism has also moved towards ordaining women in many communities.

Within Islam, women lead prayer for female-only congregations in many traditions. Sunni and Shi’a positions on women leading mixed-gender prayer vary. Most mainstream scholarship holds that women do not lead mixed congregations in formal salah, though this has been debated by progressive Muslim scholars. Women have historically been scholars of hadith and Islamic law; figures such as Aisha, the wife of the Prophet, were major religious authorities. In British Muslim communities today, women are increasingly active in mosque leadership, education and community roles.

Sikhism explicitly teaches the complete equality of women and men. The Guru Granth Sahib contains compositions by women, and Sikh teaching has consistently opposed practices that restrict women. In practice, women in Sikh communities lead prayers, read from the Guru Granth Sahib and participate fully in all aspects of gurdwara life. Amritdhari Sikh women undertake the same initiation ceremony (Amrit Sanskar) as men.

A common error is to write “Christianity teaches that women should...” as if all Christians hold the same view. The mark scheme for Theme F explicitly rewards students who name the sub-tradition — Catholic, Anglican, evangelical, Quaker, Reform Jewish, Orthodox Jewish. Each sub-tradition has a distinct position grounded in different readings of scripture and tradition. Top-band answers always name the specific sub-tradition and explain the reasoning behind its view.

The Status and Treatment of LGBTQ+ People in Religion

The spec also asks students to understand the status and treatment of those in same-sex relationships within religion. Again, different sub-traditions hold significantly different views, and those differences are themselves theologically grounded.

The Roman Catholic Church teaches, in the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1994), that marriage is a sacrament between a man and a woman. The Church does not recognise same-sex marriage and teaches that same-sex relationships are not in keeping with the natural law as it understands it, while also stating that people with same-sex attractions must be treated with respect, compassion and sensitivity. In 2024, Pope Francis approved the blessing of same-sex couples in pastoral contexts, while maintaining the Church’s teaching on marriage itself; this represents a development in pastoral practice, though not a change in doctrine.

Many Protestant and evangelical denominations hold similar teachings to the Catholic Church on marriage, grounding their view in biblical passages including Genesis 2, Romans 1, and 1 Corinthians 6. The Church of England’s official position defines marriage as being between a man and a woman, though debates within the Church are ongoing. The Methodist Church in Britain voted in 2021 to allow same-sex marriages on Methodist premises, reflecting a different reading of Christian teaching. Quaker communities affirmed same-sex marriage as early as 2009. The diversity of Christian positions on this issue is considerable.

Within Judaism, views vary equally significantly. Orthodox Judaism does not permit same-sex marriage. Reform Judaism in Britain and America affirmed same-sex marriage in 1990 and has conducted such ceremonies since. Liberal Judaism (the British Liberal movement) moved to affirm same-sex partnerships earlier still. Masorti communities differ in their approach. Students should understand that Judaism is not monolithic on this question.

Non-religious perspectives, including those of humanist and atheist organisations, generally affirm the equal moral worth and rights of LGBTQ+ people. Humanists UK supports equal marriage and argues from a position that human dignity and happiness are the basis of ethical judgement. The UDHR (Article 2) prohibits discrimination on the basis of “other status”, which many human rights lawyers have interpreted as including sexual orientation.

UDHR Article 18 protects the freedom to hold and express religious beliefs. This includes the freedom to manifest religion through worship, observance, practice and teaching. However, rights come with responsibilities: the UDHR also states that everyone has duties to the community, and that rights may be limited only to protect the rights of others or to meet just requirements of public order. In Britain, the Equality Act 2010 protects religion and belief as a protected characteristic, alongside sexual orientation and gender — meaning that different rights can sometimes come into tension in law and in public life. Religious traditions themselves vary in how they navigate this tension: some emphasise the duty to proclaim one’s faith freely; others emphasise the duty to respect the conscience and dignity of all people.

Key Fact

On women’s ordination: the Roman Catholic Church does not ordain women; the Church of England has ordained women priests since 1994 and women bishops since 2014; Orthodox Judaism does not ordain women rabbis; Reform Judaism has done so since 1972. On same-sex marriage: the Catholic Church does not recognise it; Reform Judaism affirmed it in 1990; the Methodist Church in Britain voted in 2021 to allow same-sex marriages on Methodist premises; Quaker communities affirmed same-sex marriage in 2009. These sub-tradition contrasts are essential for top-band exam answers.

title: Revelation: Visions, Miracles and Nature
content_html:
How Do People Claim to Know God?

If God exists, how might humans gain knowledge of this? Religious traditions across the world describe two broad paths: special revelation and general revelation. Both have been used to describe divine attributes — the qualities believers ascribe to God. Both have also been challenged by philosophers and non-believers. This lesson explores what these terms mean, what they reveal about the divine, and why their value is contested.

Special Revelation: Visions

Special revelation refers to direct, personal experiences in which God (or, in non-theistic traditions, ultimate reality) is believed to communicate with a specific individual. One of the most commonly cited forms is the vision. Visions are reported across religious traditions. In Christianity, the conversion of Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9) is a classic example: Saul was travelling to persecute Christians when a blinding light surrounded him and he heard the voice of Jesus. After this experience, he became Paul the Apostle and one of the most significant figures in early Christianity. Believers regard this as a direct encounter with the risen Christ — a special revelation that transformed an individual’s life and understanding.

The Marian apparitions at Lourdes in 1858 offer a second example. The 14-year-old Bernadette Soubirous reported seeing a vision of a luminous woman at the grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes who identified herself as “the Immaculate Conception.” The Catholic Church, after extensive investigation, officially recognised the apparitions in 1862. The site of Lourdes has since become one of the world’s most visited pilgrimage destinations, and the healings reported there are subject to scrutiny by a medical bureau. For Catholics, Bernadette’s vision is a genuine revelation — a direct communication from the divine to a human being.

Key Fact

Two widely cited examples of visions: (1) Saul on the road to Damascus (Acts 9) — a blinding light and the voice of Jesus led to Saul’s conversion and transformation into Paul the Apostle. (2) Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes (1858) — visions of the Virgin Mary, recognised by the Catholic Church, that established Lourdes as a major pilgrimage site.

Special Revelation: Enlightenment

Enlightenment is a distinct category of special revelation that appears across several traditions. In Buddhism, the Bodhi (awakening) of Siddhartha Gautama under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya is the paradigmatic example. The Buddha did not receive a revelation from a creator God — Buddhism does not require belief in such a God — but he attained a direct insight into the nature of reality: the Four Noble Truths and the way to end suffering. This is significant for Theme C because it illustrates how the idea of “revelation” operates differently in different traditions. For Buddhists, enlightenment is the direct realisation of truth about existence, not a message from a divine person.

In Sikh teaching, the founder Guru Nanak received a revelation from Waheguru (God) when he went to bathe in a river and did not return for three days. When he emerged, he declared: “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” Sikhs understand this as a direct divine revelation that formed the foundation of the Sikh path. The Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal Sikh scripture, is itself understood as the living word of God — revelation in written form. In Hindu mystical traditions such as Advaita Vedanta, the highest form of enlightenment (moksha) involves the direct experiential realisation that atman (the individual self) and Brahman (ultimate reality) are one.

General Revelation: Nature and Scripture

Unlike special revelation (which comes to specific individuals), general revelation is available to all people through the natural world and through reason. Many believers hold that the beauty and order of nature — the turning of seasons, the complexity of the cell, the vastness of the cosmos — communicates something about its creator. The Christian theologian Thomas Aquinas believed that natural reason could arrive at some knowledge of God through the created order, even without scripture. The Qur’an calls the natural world “ayat” (signs) of God’s existence and power: “In the creation of the heavens and earth... there are signs for those who reason” (Qur’an 3:190). Genesis 1 presents God as deliberately ordering creation: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31), suggesting that creation itself reflects God’s character.

Scripture is another form of general revelation that believers across traditions regard as a source of knowledge about the divine. The Christian Bible, the Qur’an, the Torah, and the Guru Granth Sahib are each regarded by their respective communities as containing revealed knowledge of God’s nature, will and purposes. For many believers, scripture provides a more reliable and systematic form of knowledge about God than individual mystical experience, precisely because it is accessible to all and tested by a community over time.

Religious traditions describe the divine using several key attributes. An omnipotent God has unlimited power — a quality supported by accounts of miracles and by the creation narratives in Genesis, the Qur’an and the Guru Granth Sahib. An omniscient God knows all things, including the deepest thoughts of every human being — present in Psalm 139 (“You have searched me, Lord, and you know me”) and in Islamic teaching about God’s omniscience (al-Alim).

Theistic traditions also distinguish between a personal God — one who cares for individuals, hears prayer, and acts in history — and an impersonal divine — an ultimate reality or force that does not relate to humans as a person. Many Hindu schools understand Brahman as ultimately impersonal: the ground of all existence, not a deity with feelings or intentions. Buddhism similarly does not teach a personal creator God. By contrast, Christianity, Islam, Judaism and Sikhism all describe God in strongly personal terms.

A immanent God is present within the world and within human experience: active in history, responsive to prayer, encountered in worship. A transcendent God exists beyond and above the universe: unlimited by space, time or matter. Most monotheistic traditions hold that God is both — “closer to you than your jugular vein” (Qur’an 50:16) and yet beyond full human comprehension. The tension between divine immanence and transcendence is a central theme in the philosophy of religion.

Challenges to Revelation as a Source of Knowledge

Not everyone accepts that visions, miracles and religious experiences are genuine sources of knowledge about the divine. Several challenges deserve careful consideration. First, different revelatory experiences lead to contradictory conclusions about the divine — some describe a personal God, others an impersonal ultimate reality, others a universe without any creator at all. If revelation were a reliable source of knowledge, we might expect greater agreement. Philosophers such as John Hick have grappled with this, arguing that all religious experiences may be culturally shaped encounters with the same ultimate reality.

Second, there is always the possibility that those who claim to have had visions or miraculous experiences were lying or mistaken. Hume argued that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and personal testimony — especially from centuries ago — does not meet this standard. Modern psychology offers natural explanations for mystical experiences: they may result from unusual brain states, sensory deprivation, grief, or temporal lobe activity. The philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach argued that “God” is a human projection — what we value most in ourselves, projected onto the cosmos.

Humanists and atheists typically hold that reported visions and religious experiences, however sincere, do not provide reliable evidence of an objective divine reality. They point out that the specific content of religious experiences consistently reflects the cultural background of the person having them — a medieval Christian is unlikely to report an encounter with Waheguru, and a devout Sikh is unlikely to report seeing the Virgin Mary. This cultural conditioning, non-religious thinkers argue, suggests the experience originates in the human mind rather than in an external divine source. The appropriate response to claims of special revelation is, on this view, respectful scepticism and a search for natural explanations.

Key Fact

Four key divine attributes: omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), immanent (present within the world and in human experience), transcendent (beyond and above the universe). Most monotheistic traditions — Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Sikhism — hold that God is all four simultaneously. Some Hindu schools and Buddhist teachings describe the divine as impersonal rather than personal.

title: Arguments Against the Existence of God
content_html:
Does Suffering Challenge Belief in God?

If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and entirely good, why does suffering exist? This question — known as the problem of evil — is one of the oldest and most persistent arguments against the existence of God. Alongside it, the findings of modern science have been used to argue that a creator God is unnecessary. Together, these represent the most serious challenges that believers must respond to. This lesson examines both challenges and the responses that religious traditions offer.

Types of Evil and Suffering

Philosophers distinguish two types of evil. Natural evil includes suffering caused by events like earthquakes, tsunamis, cancer, and famine — things that happen regardless of human action. Moral evil refers to suffering caused by human choices: war, genocide, abuse, cruelty. The philosopher J.L. Mackie argued in his 1955 essay “Evil and Omnipotence” that the existence of evil is logically inconsistent with an all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good God. If God is able to prevent evil (omnipotence), knows about evil (omniscience) and wants to prevent it (omnibenevolence), then evil should not exist. Its existence, Mackie argued, means at least one of those divine attributes must be false — or God does not exist.

Key Fact

Natural evil = suffering from nature (earthquakes, disease). Moral evil = suffering from human choices (war, murder). J.L. Mackie argued that the existence of either type is logically inconsistent with a God who is omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing) and omnibenevolent (all-good).

Christian Responses to the Problem of Evil

Christian theology has developed several responses to the problem of evil. The soul-making theodicy — associated with the philosopher John Hick and drawing on the early Christian thinker Irenaeus — argues that God permits suffering because it is the necessary condition for human moral and spiritual growth. Just as muscles strengthen through resistance, character develops through challenge. A world without suffering would be a world without the opportunity to develop courage, compassion, or perseverance. Irenaeus described humanity as made “in the image of God” but not yet fully in the “likeness of God” — suffering is part of the journey towards that likeness.

The free will defence — developed by Alvin Plantinga — argues that God created humans with genuine freedom to choose between good and evil. Moral evil is the result of people misusing that freedom. A world in which God prevented every act of evil would require removing human free will, and a world of puppets doing only what God programmes them to do would have less moral worth than a world of genuinely free agents. Many Christians draw on Genesis 3 (the Fall) to explain how human sin entered the world through Adam and Eve’s free choice to disobey God.

In Islam, suffering is understood within the framework of qadar (divine decree). Muslims hold that God is entirely just and that all suffering ultimately serves God’s purposes, even when humans cannot understand them. Suffering is seen as a test from God: “We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits” (Qur’an 2:155). Patient endurance (sabr) in the face of suffering is itself a form of worship. Islam also emphasises that natural evil does not originate from a devil equal to God — there is no dualism; God alone is ultimate.

In Jewish tradition, the problem of suffering is powerfully explored in the Book of Job. Job is a righteous man who loses everything — family, health, wealth — not as punishment for sin but as a test. Job’s response is to continue trusting God even when he cannot understand why he suffers. Jewish theology does not offer a single theodicy but encourages wrestling with the question honestly. After the Holocaust, many Jewish thinkers such as Elie Wiesel and Emil Fackenheim engaged deeply with the question of how God could permit such suffering, with varying conclusions about faith and protest.

Arguments Based on Science

Alongside the problem of evil, modern science has provided alternative accounts of the universe’s origin and development that some argue make the existence of a creator God unnecessary. The Big Bang theory, developed through the work of Georges Lemaître, Edwin Hubble and others in the 20th century, describes the universe as originating in an extraordinarily rapid expansion from an extremely dense initial state approximately 13.8 billion years ago. This is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: the observed expansion of the universe, the cosmic microwave background radiation, and the relative abundance of light elements.

Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection, set out in On the Origin of Species (1859), explained how the diversity and complexity of living organisms developed over billions of years through random variation and the survival of the fittest. Atheist scientists and philosophers such as Richard Dawkins argue that evolution removes the need for a designer God: once we understand how complex life arises through natural selection, the Design argument loses its force. The universe, on this view, is explicable entirely in terms of natural causes.

Many students write that “science has proved God does not exist.” This is inaccurate and loses marks. Science describes how the universe operates through natural processes; it cannot, in principle, disprove the existence of a being outside or beyond the universe. What science does is remove the necessity of a God-explanation for specific things — the origin of species, the age of the Earth — by providing natural explanations. Many religious believers, including the Catholic Church (which teaches that evolution and Big Bang cosmology are compatible with belief in God as creator), accept the findings of science while continuing to believe. The debate between science and religion is more nuanced than a simple clash.

Atheist and Humanist Perspectives

For atheists, the combination of the problem of evil and scientific explanation makes belief in God unnecessary and unjustified. The ancient Greek formulation attributed to Epicurus is still quoted: if God is willing to prevent evil but unable, God is not omnipotent; if God is able but unwilling, God is not good; if God is both willing and able, why does evil exist? Bertrand Russell famously stated that there is no sufficient reason to believe in God and that the problem of evil in particular makes the idea of a benevolent creator implausible.

Humanism, as represented in the UK by Humanists UK, holds that human beings can live ethical, meaningful lives through reason, compassion and humanity alone, without the need for religious belief or a divine lawgiver. Humanists do not regard the problem of evil as a dilemma they need to resolve — they simply do not begin with the assumption that an all-powerful, all-good God exists. For humanists, suffering is a natural fact of a universe governed by physical laws, and the appropriate response is human solidarity and action to reduce suffering, not prayer or theodicy.

Key Fact

The free will defence: God gave humans genuine freedom to choose; moral evil is humans misusing that freedom, not God’s fault. Counter-argument: free will does not explain natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — these are not caused by human choice.

title: Arguments For the Existence of God
content_html:
Can Reason Prove God Exists?

For centuries, philosophers and theologians have asked whether reason alone can demonstrate that God exists. Three classic arguments have shaped this debate: the Design argument, the First Cause argument, and the argument from miracles. Each attempts to move from things we can observe in the world to a conclusion about God’s existence. Each has also attracted powerful objections. This lesson explores all three, so that you can evaluate them fairly.

Key Fact

The three main arguments for God’s existence are: the Design argument (associated with William Paley, 1802), the First Cause argument (associated with Thomas Aquinas, 13th century), and the argument from miracles. All three draw on evidence from the world around us rather than from scripture alone.

The Design Argument (Teleological Argument)

The Design argument holds that the universe shows signs of purpose and order that are best explained by a designer. The philosopher William Paley presented this vividly in Natural Theology (1802) through his famous watchmaker analogy. Paley argued that if you found a watch on a heath and examined its cogs and springs working together to tell the time, you would immediately conclude the watch had a designer. The natural world, with its intricate ecosystems, the human eye, the precise conditions that allow life on Earth, shows the same complexity. Therefore, Paley reasoned, just as the watch demands a watchmaker, the universe demands a divine designer — whom Christians, Muslims, Jews and Sikhs identify as God.

Contemporary thinkers such as Richard Swinburne have developed the teleological argument, pointing to the fine-tuning of physical constants in the universe as evidence that its orderliness requires explanation. From a Christian perspective, Genesis 1 portrays God deliberately creating and ordering the world — “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). Many believers see in the structure of nature a sign of God’s creative intelligence.

Strengths: The argument is based on observable evidence. It matches the intuition many people have when they look at the natural world — that it seems designed. Philosophers such as F.R. Tennant highlighted that the universe appears fine-tuned to permit life in a way that seems too precise to be coincidence.

Weaknesses: David Hume, writing before Paley in Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, challenged the analogy: a watch is made of parts put together by human hands, but the universe is not like a watch. Hume also noted that the universe might have many designers, not one; that poor design in nature (disease, natural disasters) might suggest an imperfect or uncaring designer; and that an analogy is not proof. Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection (1859) offered an alternative explanation for biological complexity — the appearance of design can arise through random variation and the survival of organisms best adapted to their environment, without any designer being needed.

The First Cause Argument (Cosmological Argument)

Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian, developed a series of arguments for God’s existence that he presented in his major work Summa Theologiae. The second of his Five Ways addresses causation. Aquinas observed that in the world everything that exists is caused by something before it. A flame burns wood; the wood was grown from a seed; the seed came from a tree. This chain cannot go back forever — an infinite chain of causes, Aquinas argued, would never have got started. There must be a First Cause that began the chain of causation but was not itself caused. This uncaused first cause, Aquinas reasoned, is what people call God.

Islamic theology makes a similar argument: the kalam cosmological argument holds that everything that begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause outside itself, which is God. Jewish theology also holds that God is the uncaused creator (Bore olam — Creator of the universe). Across these traditions, the First Cause argument reinforces the monotheistic conviction that God exists necessarily, not contingently.

Strengths: The argument uses logical reasoning. It aligns with the Big Bang cosmological model, which suggests the universe did have a beginning. Many scientists accept that something caused the Big Bang, even if they disagree about what that something was. Philosopher Alvin Plantinga has argued that God is the only plausible candidate for a necessary, uncaused being.

Weaknesses: Bertrand Russell argued that the universe may simply exist without needing a cause — “The universe is just there, and that’s all.” If everything requires a cause, what caused God? Aquinas’s response is that God, by definition, is uncaused — a necessary being — but critics argue this is an assertion rather than a proof. The argument may also prove only that something caused the universe, not that this cause is the personal God of Christianity or Islam.

The Argument from Miracles

The third argument holds that miracles — events that seem to violate the normal laws of nature — provide evidence that a powerful God acts in the world. Aquinas defined a miracle as something done by God that nature could not do on its own. For Christians, the resurrection of Jesus is the central miracle: on the third day after his crucifixion, the Gospels record that Jesus rose from the dead (Luke 24:1–12). If this happened as reported, it represents God’s direct intervention in the physical world and is the foundation of Christian belief in eternal life.

A second widely cited example is the healing miracles attributed to the shrine at Lourdes, France, where in 1858 a young girl named Bernadette Soubirous reported a series of visions of the Virgin Mary. Since then, the Catholic Church has officially recognised 70 miraculous healings at Lourdes after rigorous medical scrutiny, including cases where patients recovered from conditions doctors could not explain. Believers argue these healings point to God’s continuing power to act in the world.

Key Fact

The argument from miracles says: if miracles occur — events that break the laws of nature — they require a supernatural cause; God is the only adequate supernatural cause; therefore God exists. The resurrection of Jesus (Luke 24) and the healings at Lourdes (from 1858) are cited as examples by Christians.

Strengths and Weaknesses of the Argument from Miracles

David Hume raised a powerful challenge in Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748). He argued that it is always more probable that the witness to a miracle was mistaken, deceived, or lying than that the laws of nature were actually broken. Hume also noted that people in many cultures report miracles on behalf of contradictory religions — they cannot all be right, which undermines the evidential value of miracle accounts. Philosophers such as J.L. Mackie developed this critique further, arguing that reliable scientific evidence for a law of nature will always outweigh the testimony of individual witnesses.

Believers respond that dismissing all miraculous reports on principle is itself a bias. They argue that where many independent witnesses report the same unexplained event, testimony deserves serious weight. From a non-religious perspective, however, humanists and atheists typically explain apparently miraculous events through unknown natural causes, misdiagnosis, spontaneous remission, or psychological factors. For humanists, the world is governed entirely by natural laws and there is no credible scientific evidence for supernatural intervention.
